title_original: Routes Into Park Royal
editorial_excerpt_zh: For the inaugural Manufactory x ArtReview Writer’s Residency, Aram Masharqa traces how transport, industry and migration have shaped one of London’s strangest districts.

article_text:
For the inaugural Manufactory x ArtReview Writer’s Residency, Aram Masharqa traces how transport, industry and migration have shaped one of London’s strangest districts.

Park Royal, the largest existing industrial estate in the UK is a product of London’s rapid northwestern expansion in the twentieth century. Although infrastructure was never explicitly planned for the area, the railways and the canal that run through it provided the justification for Park Royal’s industrial development. Its first factories produced munitions for the First World War; later came all manner of other industries and businesses: the Guinness brewery, Renault’s car plant and, the only one still operating, McVitie’s round-the-clock biscuit production.

The A40 cuts directly through Park Royal and should have been a major driver of its rapid development. Instead, the narrow roads and alleyways of the industrial park itself couldn’t sustain the immense volume of traffic the A40 facilitated, and many factories relocated outside London. By an accident of timing, this decline coincided with the Lebanese Civil War, and many Lebanese immigrants settled around Park Royal, giving the area a new character that it retains today in its Arab supermarkets (Goodies is a local favourite) and countless shisha lounges. Now, plans for a new HS2 transport hub in nearby Old Oak Common mean the estate is earmarked for a whole new wave of development.

So, there is a Park Royal of the canal, of the trains, and of the motorways, each of them slightly different. I began travelling there by a different mode of transport each time, as a way to try and get closer to an area whose history has been shaped by movement: of goods, workers, industries, residents. Though I grew up nearby in Sudbury, my relationship to Park Royal as a ‘local’ has changed over the years. And in starting this project, I also became a temporary participant in the contemporary arts ecosystem housed in the various studio buildings nestled between the industrial estate’s warehouses, factories and logistics centres. Moving through the area in different ways became a way of looking again at a place I thought I knew, and of asking what its roads, railways and waterways might reveal about the communities and economies that have accumulated around them.

Entry 1: Walking the Grand Union Canal

Some time after I was old enough to explore London on my own, the canal came to my attention as a public access route. At that point, I knew Park Royal mainly as the Royale Leisure Park, which we only referred to by its amenities: the cinema, the gym, the Chinese buffet that is now a shisha lounge, and most importantly, the bowling alley. This was Park Royal to me: south of the A40, its identity reinforced by the proximity of the Park Royal underground station. The Big ASDA supermarket and the industrial park, meanwhile, would always be in an area known to me as ‘Deep Park Royal’, sitting north of the A40.

The canal, built more than a century before the motorway, cuts straight into Deep Park Royal. For much of the towpath, tall hedges and fencing obscure what lies beyond, until they abruptly stop and open onto a view of seemingly infinite rows of industrial buildings. Here the path splits: one route continues along the canal, while the other bends into the estate, as though anticipating some public interest in the warehouse district. When I was younger, I heeded this perceived obligation to explore, wandering the industrial alleyways until the confused looks of the workers – usually in high-vis, hard hats, or long white coats – gave me the feeling that I had strayed into a back-of-house I wasn’t supposed to see.

Even now, knowing more about Park Royal, there is something strange about this junction, where the quaint and scenic meets the sights and sounds of industry. The contrast owes more to the canal’s changing function than to Park Royal itself, but the friction between the two speaks to a tension underpinning the entire district, and reveals something about the area as a whole. Park Royal is both a front- and back-of-house: a place of public leisure and private labour, familiar amenities and largely unseen systems of production.

Entry 2: Park Royal Tube Station

You would be forgiven for assuming, as I did, that Park Royal Underground Station is the nearest to the industrial park. This was the stop I knew from childhood, for easy access to the glorious retail park. Exiting the station and checking the map for my destination, I stared longingly over the impenetrable six-lane motorway. On a nicer day, I might have walked through the subway and down Coronation Road to the industrial park, but that day the muggy, overcast grey was enough to justify chartering an e-bike.

Park Royal Station, the subway beneath the A40, and the fact that the nearest station to the industrial park is called North Acton, are all the products of Park Royal’s piecemeal development. The first station was Park Royal & Twyford Abbey Station, built to serve the Royal Agricultural Show and surviving now only as a modest bridge over Twyford Abbey Road. Later, two stations on the Great Western Rail’s Acton-Northolt line – Park Royal Station and Park Royal West Halt – served the industrial side of the district; both have since closed. The route might now be little more than a historical footnote were it not for Old Oak Common, once connected to the line and soon to become an HS2 superhub. Perhaps, then, just as the subway once connected the new Park Royal tube station to the old railway station, Old Oak Common will generate another geography of footpaths, alleyways, and subways. I’m not convinced it will make Park Royal any less strange, or any more orderly.

Entry 3: Drive directly in at night

The ease with which I turn off the A40 onto the now relatively quiet streets reminds me that this is the method of transport the industrial estate was built to handle. This section of the A40 is called the Western Avenue and, much like the trains, it is something of a stub. It was intended to connect to a wider network of inner-city elevated motorways called the Ringways, but almost none of them were built. Except for a series of concrete motorways that bisect entire neighbourhoods in West London. If Park Royal doesn’t quite feel like ‘London’, perhaps that’s because it belongs to a vision of a distinctly more American London, one that hedged all its bets on the mighty car.

The evening air is filled with anticipation as rows of cars, rather than lorries and HGVs, line the streets. Double parking is common outside the countless food trucks and Shisha lounges. Writing for London’s Kitchen , a 2021 project and publication exploring Park Royal’s industry, culture and changing character, Zarina Muhammad describes these lounges as emblematic of a new kind of ‘Dinner and Dances’, referring to a former staple of Asian-British Muslim life in the banqueting halls in Northwest London, where all manner of social events were held. Maybe it’s because I’m alone, maybe it’s because I’m in a version of London which I never fully got to know, or maybe I can’t bear the awkwardness as the men at the Shisha lounge puzzle at my broken Arabic, but either way I don’t stay at the lounge, I don’t even park.

The roads, the lounges, the parking: Park Royal is almost like being back in Jordan’s East Amman, in an area called Marka, also known for its haphazard parking, late-night shawarma, and all-round anarchic atmosphere. One is almost like the other, and Park Royal seems to relish this ‘almost’. Almost, because a shisha lounge might sit next to a smash burger truck, opposite an English pub bordering the Grand Union Canal, with the McVitie’s logo shining from the factory just across the way. It sounds planned; it almost sounds ‘English’, in a multicultural-pluralist kind of way. But it is only almost-planned, which is to say, not planned at all. It is an indefinitely temporary place for all those who have made a home in the almost.

Aram Masharqa is a London-based Palestinian writer.

article_text:
Jennifer Lawrence appeared on the latest episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast and spoke out for the first time about what it was like to reprise Katniss Everdeen for the first time in 11 years. The Oscar winner is back as her iconic “Hunger Games” character in the upcoming prequel movie “Sunrise on the Reaping,” in theaters Nov. 20 from Lionsgate.

“It was unbelievable,” Lawrence said about reprising Katniss. “It was so crazy. It was the same crew. It was the same AD, who I’ve worked with a million times because I love him. And with Josh [Hutcherson] and Woody [Harrelson] … it was so emotional. Josh and I didn’t walk to the bathroom without our arms around each other. It was so beautiful. And Woody, obviously, came through the window of my hotel room uninvited. It wouldn’t be the same if he listened to boundaries or used a door.”

Related Stories

Guillermo del Toro Tears Up as He Says ‘We’re Handing Down a World in Ruins’: ‘It Pains Me Deeply to See Three Generations Fail the Next’

Variety reported last December that Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson were returning as Katniss and Peeta Mellark for a scene in “Sunrise on the Reaping.” Lawrence has now let it slip that Woody Harrelson will also be back as Haymitch. The new prequel movie centers on a young Haymitch (played by Joseph Zada) as he competes in the 50th Hunger Games. Book readers know that Suzanne Collins’ “Sunrise on the Reaping” novel ends with a flash-forward epilogue featuring Katniss, Peeta and Haymitch, so it appears the film adpatation is following suit.

Lawrence told Variety during her “No Hard Feelings” press tour in 2023 that she was “totally” open to reprising her “Hunger Games” role of Katniss Everdeen should the right opportunity arise. She added at the time, “If Katniss ever could ever come back into my life, 100 percent.”

As Katniss, Lawrence headlined four “Hunger Games” movies between 2012 and 2015. The franchise (which also includes the Rachel Zegler-led 2023 prequel “The Ballad of Songbirds & Snakes”) has grossed $3.3 billion to date at the worldwide box office.

“What made me nervous was how it could negatively affect my acting career and my personal life,” Lawrence said on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast about her biggest concern with joining the franchise when she was 20 years old. “The one thing I was always sure of when I was younger was that I wanted to be a mom, and this looked so different then doing some indies. ‘Twilight’ had just come out and everybody saw what that was. It was more like… how is this going to change my life and my acting career?”

Watch Lawrence’s full interview on the “Call Her Daddy” podcast in the video below.

article_text:
Bela Bajaria is out at Netflix .

The news comes only 24 hours after the streamer underwent a massive cull, laying off around 1,000 employees .

Bajaria joined the company in 2016 , initially running its unscripted TV slate, and was named Chief Content Officer in January 2023 .

Related Stories

Netflix Names Peter Rice As Chief Content Officer

Netflix Layoffs Underway, Streamer Cutting 1,000 Jobs, 6% Of Workforce

There have been rumors about her being axed by the company for the past couple of weeks, all denied by Netflix. Former Disney exec Peter Rice has replaced her .

Watch on Deadline

RELATED: Netflix’s Bela Bajaria Has No Regrets Over Failed Warners Buy: “It Was Always A Nice To Have At A Certain Price”

It comes amid slowing growth for the streamer. Netflix’s stock price has dropped more than 40% over the past year (off 25% year to date) as Wall Street has increasingly scrutinized its viewer engagement, which increased only 2% over the first half of the year to 97 billion hours viewed.

Co-CEO Ted Sarandos said recently at the Bloomberg Screentime event , “At the time we said that, I think we were pretty unsophisticated about how we talked about engagement. Meaning, in that world, all the revenue is equal, a profit is equal, all engagement is equal, and all engagement is not equal. We are growing engagement, on 200 billion hours of watching, we grew 2% in our last announcement.”

RELATED: List Of Hollywood & Media Layoffs From Paramount To Warner Bros Discovery To CNN & More

Netflix also has been struggling with ratings for its returning series, many of which have posted season-to-season viewership declines, including Beef and The Four Seasons . On its last earnings video, Sarandos claimed that it actually has improved this problem this year and said it was “very common” in the industry. Such issues, however, and the fact that Netflix has not launched a big zeitgeisty title in over a year, can’t have helped Bajaria’s cause.

“I want to thank Bela for a decade of dedication, innovation, creativity and leadership,” said co-CEO Ted Sarandos, who broke the news to Netflix staff in an internal memo (read it below).. “She led enormous changes at Netflix. She helped broaden our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports, in addition to crafting and running a world class, global slate of films and series. I’m incredibly grateful for everything she’s done to help Netflix entertain the world.”

He listed hit series Bajaria had commissioned during the various stages of her Netflix tenure, from launching the streamer’s unscripted business with shows like the Queer Eye reboot and partnering with traditional studios on shows such as You early on to overseeing international (L upin, Squid Game ) and adding UCAN ( The Diplomat, The Night Agent ) and sports/live programming (WWE, Tyson vs Paul, the NFL).

RELATED: Netflix Layoffs Affect Unscripted Casting & Development Execs Impacted

Here is Sarandos’ internal email in full:

Hi everyone, I have an important update to share about our Content leadership. After a phenomenal decade at Netflix, Bela is leaving the company. It’s hard to overstate the impact Bela has had during her time here. From expanding our content offering to include the large-scale expansion of unscripted programming and the launches of live events and sports to helping shape the broadening of our content offering around the world. So much of what you see on Netflix today can be traced back to a Bela initiative: Insatiable, Queer Eye, Lupin, You, The Diplomat, WWE , YuYu Hakusho, The Night Agent, Heeramandi: The Diamond Bazaar, Squid Game, Tyson vs Paul, Cien años de soledad , the NFL. She also helped reshape our strategy to focus on fewer, bigger, better movies, championing films like KPop Demon Hunters, The Adventures of Cliff Booth, and Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew, as well as bringing award winning films like La Bola Negra and Possible Love to Netflix. A tremendous and diverse range of content (and that’s just a snapshot), bringing joy to our members across so many genres. Bela has built and shaped a truly global Content organization, hiring brilliant people and empowering them to make good decisions. I am incredibly grateful to her for everything she’s done. I know this is a big change in a year that has already had its share. But I also see an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in UCAN where we have an outsize impact in creating big, buzzy hits that our members love and drive conversation around the world. To help us seize on this moment, I’m excited to share that we’ve hired a new leader. Peter Rice is joining Netflix as our new Chief Content Officer beginning next week. Peter is one of the most effective at-scale operators in the entertainment industry. His business acumen is sharp, his talent relationships are exceptionally strong, and his experience across both TV and film is deep and broad. On the film side, running Fox Searchlight, he helped bring beloved fan favorite films like Slumdog Millionaire, Little Miss Sunshine, Sideways and Juno to screens. And more recently, as Chairman of Walt Disney Television, he led one of the most successful television divisions in the world, where he was responsible for a massive breadth and scale of shows ranging from The Simpsons, American Idol ,and Modern Family, to The Bear, and Abbott Elementary, along with ABC News programming and major sporting events such as the Super Bowl, NBA Finals and FIFA World Cup Finals. He’s one of the few people in our industry who has ever operated at the quality and scale that we do at Netflix every day. In the last few years, he has turned his attention to creating and has produced films with Alex Garland, Danny Boyle, Chris Rock, Jason Reitman and Aaron Sorkin at Sony and A24. I’ve gotten to know Peter personally over the years, and I’ve always been impressed by his straightforward approach, the depth of his relationships and his exceptional creative and business instincts. Talent should have the best experiences of their life here, and Peter and I both believe that Netflix can and should be the home of the best storytellers in the world. It’s been an eventful series of days here, and I realize we’ve asked you to absorb a lot of news and a lot of information. But we all know change is what we do at Netflix. Greg and I will host a companywide town hall on Wednesday, October 21. I want everyone to hear how we’re thinking about the strategy and our execution amid this week’s changes, and to have a chance to ask questions. It will be informal and mostly Q&A, so please bring your questions about this week’s changes and anything else on your mind. Please join me in thanking Bela, and welcoming Peter to the team. Ted

article_text:
Source: Debbie Zhou

Katie Goodson-Thomas

Longtime Searchlight Pictures executive Katie Goodson-Thomas is joining London-based LuckyChap International as president of film.

Goodson-Thomas, presently executive vice president, co-head of production and development at Searchlight Pictures, will lead the film slate of LuckyChap International, in partnership with co-managing directors Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi, from January 2027.

“Goodson-Thomas’s deep roots in the UK film industry and extensive experience operating within the global studio system will be invaluable in expanding the company’s fast-growing film slate, and amplifying the company’s international ambitions,” said LuckyChap’s US team of Margot Robbie, Tom Ackerley, Josey McNamara and Milan Popelka, to whom she will report.

“[She] brings together world-class producer instincts, deep creative relationships across the UK and Europe, and an understanding of how to identify distinctive stories and filmmakers with the potential to travel globally – without losing the cultural specificity and creative ambition that makes them compelling.”

Since joining Searchlight in 2015, Goodson-Thomas has overseen titles including Yorgos Lanthimos’ The Favourite and Poor Things , Martin McDonagh’s Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri , The Banshees Of Inisherin and the upcoming Wild Horse Nine , as well as Andrew Haigh’s All Of Us Strangers and Alice Birch’s upcoming directorial debut Sweetsick starring Cate Blanchett, a co-production with Tessa Ross’s House Productions.

“We’re in awe of everything Katie has accomplished throughout her career, and we all feel extraordinarily privileged that she is bringing her undeniable creative talents, vision and depth of experience to LuckyChap International,” added the LuckyChap US partners.

“She’s such a kindred spirit culturally, and we’ve long admired her ability to spot exceptional filmmaking talent and champion their projects from the very beginning all the way through. We genuinely couldn’t be more excited to have her join us on this adventure, and to forge a killer slate together that we can all be incredibly proud of.”

LuckyChap International was set up in November 2025 as a joint venture with France-based European studio group Mediawan to operate in the UK and across Europe. Mona Qureshi, a former director of scripted series at Netflix UK, and Tanya Qureshi, previously drama commissioning editor at the BBC, have led the company to date with a focus on TV.

“[Goodson-Thomas’s] career embodies the kind of independent spirit and big-heartedness that inspires us, and her ambition, taste and creative instinct make her a natural fit for what we are building,” said Mona Qureshi and Tanya Qureshi. “We can’t wait to have her alongside us as a fellow journeywoman.”

LuckyChap majority owns the company and has credits including Saltburn , Barbie and Wuthering Heights. Upcoming titles include Rich Peppiatt’s Kneecap follow-up Bad Bridgets , with Trevor Birney’s Coup d’Etat Films, now in post after a Belfast shoot for Netflix.

Goodson-Thomas joined Graham Broadbent and Damian Jones’ Dragon Pictures in 1996. She went on to work with Jon Finn on the stage version of Billy Elliott , before roles at David Thompson’s Origin Pictures and Chris Coen’s Unanimous Pictures.

“The LuckyChap team has exceptional taste, fearlessness and a creative identity entirely its own, as well as an infectious sense of possibility about what the company can achieve,” said Goodson-Thomas. “Searchlight has been such an incredible creative home for me that I always knew it would take somewhere truly special to tempt me away. The opportunity to join that alongside Mona, Tanya and such a brilliant team was simply too exciting to resist. The UK and Europe are full of remarkable talent, and I’m hugely ambitious about what we can find, back and get made together.”

“Business as usual”

Searchlight Pictures told Screen it is “business as usual” in London, with Pete Spencer, vice president of production and development, reporting directly to Los Angeles-based DanTram Nguyen, executive vice president and head of film production and development.

“Katie has been a wonderful colleague all of these years and LuckyChap International is getting an exceptional and passionate advocate for filmmakers,” said Matthew Greenfield, president of Searchlight Pictures.

“We couldn’t be happier for her as she takes on this next chapter, and we’re excited to see all that she and the team will accomplish together.”

title_zh: 《事到如今還談什麼愛》：有時候，我們也說愛的組成是火花
summary_zh: 来源摘录：作家書寫故事，總是以愛之外的事物形容著愛。當一個作家被問起愛究竟是什麼，她往往只能語塞，這會不會是人的組成，本就有千萬種可能，而小詩身上的特質，恰好是她必須戮力尋找脈絡、證據，才能透過具體事物表述她的愛。橫亙於戀人之間的事物，其實只是個體之間本就有著距離。而愛在語言之後，會不會就失去它本身的有機了？ 這篇文章 《事到如今還談什麼愛》：有時候，我們也說愛的組成是火花 最早出現於 釀電影 。

"https://filmaholic.tw/people/683de039fd89780001db6704/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "這樣的活力，很大一部分來自小詩的有機。 比如，在杜夫談起生育的未來，小詩幾次以玩笑迴避，或者在上樓睡覺前，她只是將毛毯隨手扔在客廳的地板上。小詩身上所具備的能動性，當然有著令人難以忍受的部分，面對重要討論總是閃爍其詞的態度，如果放在真實生活裡，大概也不會讓人感覺討喜。任性，隨心所欲，自私。不過又有點可愛，有點迷人。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "尤其，在杜夫又想繼續討論生育計畫卻被拒，杜夫説出：「這時代的女性也該好好地融入社會。」時，這難道不是當代女性困境的證明之一嗎？即使杜夫比多數男性還要來得不「典型」。"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": 撰文／黃曦 劇照提供／台北金馬影展執行委員會 責任編輯／黃曦 核稿編輯／黃曦

「わがままで、ずるくて、だけど愛おしい。」

任性，隨心所欲，自私。狡猾，奸詐。不過又有點可愛，有點迷人。 這是寫在《事到如今還談什麼愛》（Between Two Lovers，2026）製作公司「分福」（BUNBUKU）官網上，關於作品的第一個介紹。

更多關於作品的介紹，可能是在導演廣瀨奈奈子身後，有著師承 是枝裕和 、曾任《我的意外爸爸》（Like Father, Like Son，2013）、 《比海還深》（After the Storm，2016） 副導演的經歷；不過《事到如今還談什麼愛》同樣也能貼上幾道嚴肅的議題標籤，比如日本同性婚姻現況、未婚女性／女同志伴侶代孕議題等。

《事到如今還談什麼愛》作為一部屬於當代的家庭電影，更精準地説，它是關於當代愛情的家庭電影。 自電影開場，我們首先看見小詩（ 長澤雅美 飾）、杜夫（柄本佑飾）的婚姻關係，他們的婚姻談不上激情，不過卻能讓人感受到一種活力。

這樣的活力，很大一部分來自小詩的有機。 比如，在杜夫談起生育的未來，小詩幾次以玩笑迴避，或者在上樓睡覺前，她只是將毛毯隨手扔在客廳的地板上。小詩身上所具備的能動性，當然有著令人難以忍受的部分，面對重要討論總是閃爍其詞的態度，如果放在真實生活裡，大概也不會讓人感覺討喜。任性，隨心所欲，自私。不過又有點可愛，有點迷人。

我想這就是原因了，小詩在進入傳統異性戀家庭結構之後，她同時出現了女人面對家庭議題時可能有的困惑，卻仍擁有／保有她只是作為自己時的慧黠。狡猾，奸詐。不過又有點可愛，有點迷人。

尤其，在杜夫又想繼續討論生育計畫卻被拒，杜夫説出：「這時代的女性也該好好地融入社會。」時，這難道不是當代女性困境的證明之一嗎？即使杜夫比多數男性還要來得不「典型」。

這對不那麼典型的伴侶，面對的依然是婚育不脫鉤的傳統家庭觀念，甚至在小詩拿起保險套、欲與杜夫更進一步發展性關係卻被拒絕時，性依然與生育彼此困囿。其後出現的英文片名「Between Two Lovers」，我們可能會以為橫亙於愛之間的，依然是這道百年難解的婚育生活。

《事到如今還談什麼愛》電影劇照／劇照提供：台北金馬影展執行委員會

不過，導演廣瀨奈奈子也同樣慧黠，圍繞上述的困境、直面上述的衝突，都可能會讓電影顯得沉悶、生硬，但在圍繞著日本女同志婚育處境的議題之上，透過編劇的輕巧、詼諧，於是觀眾可以想見一種可能性是： 我們會不會有沮喪之外的選擇？

開場不久後的發展，繪本作家小詩向杜夫坦承自己的女同志身分，並且和她的責任編輯潤奈（石橋靜河飾）已秘密戀愛六年。小詩的出櫃戲，透過兩人荒唐得令人發笑的詰問，鬆動了此類敘事經常出現的爭執，反而更進一步地討論起了結婚的意義。

小詩向杜夫提到，因為他不是一個無禮的人，因為他不是一個和普遍男性一樣的人⋯⋯，杜夫卻是反問她，難道只有這樣嗎？

但是，這樣還不夠嗎？或者，我們應該換句話說，杜夫想聽到的，肯定是愛吧？只不過，愛在語言之後，會不會就失去它本身的有機了？

作家書寫一個故事，總是以愛之外的事物形容著愛。當一個作家被問起愛究竟是什麼，她往往只能語塞，這會不會是人的組成，本就有千萬種可能，而小詩身上的特質，恰好是她必須戮力尋找脈絡、證據，才能透過具體事物表述她的愛。

橫亙於戀人之間的事物，其實就只是兩個個體之間，本就有著距離。 對一個人來說，光只是說愛是不夠的，而對另一個人來說，光只是闡明性格的優點是不夠的，所以「距離」也不過就是組成的差異罷了。

《事到如今還談什麼愛》電影劇照／劇照提供：台北金馬影展執行委員會

隨著小詩的同志身分曝光，杜夫當然也有過要她做選擇的時候，而在劇情中段，更因為杜夫和潤奈同樣都想要生孩子，於是小詩提出了不如三人共同孕育孩子的想法。

即使潤奈一直對於小詩步入婚姻的決定充滿困惑，更說出「真貨會抵抗社會，假貨才融入社會」的想法，杜夫也同樣排斥小詩的提議，但這一男一女依然周旋在他們共同的戀人之間。

我尤其喜歡三人在居家生活時的衣著，小詩總是穿著不同圖案的貓咪 T 恤，杜夫穿著的卻是一隻狗，而潤奈偶有幾件同樣是貓咪圖案的居家衣。

但是他們誰都沒養寵物，卻也心照不宣地成為了自己所身著的動物，而其中未見性愛發生在小詩各自與潤奈、杜夫的戀愛關係裡，實際上淡化了性愛在不同性別對象上（可能）產生的張力，也可能讓我們有機會以個體的目光，平等地看見三人之間的情感流動。

不過，我們的確會在回到個體處境時，依然看見其性別身分／職業身分所帶來的困境。

小詩的繪本作家身分，泰半時間都是在家工作，伴侶便認為她的職業需求剛好適合在家準備孕產、照顧孩子；杜夫面對著職場交好的男同事，看著別人的家已經有了三個孩子，他自己也受困於婚育結構所帶來的窘迫；潤奈作為未步入異性戀婚姻的女同志，她的（安全的）生育權被法律所剝奪，其後成為未婚懷孕的上班族女性，也可能受困於傳統社會的目光。

《事到如今還談什麼愛》電影劇照／劇照提供：台北金馬影展執行委員會

關於非婚生子女的權利問題，以及日本針對單身女性、女同志伴侶能否透過人工授精進行生育的現行法律討論，也讓故事延伸至最初的愛情之外。

在《事到如今還談什麼愛》裡，它同樣回到關於婚姻的討論。沒有締結異性戀婚姻的單身女性、女同志伴侶，在現實社會裡僅能尋求海外的合法管道，或者透過身邊的男同志友人、甚至網路上風險性極高的仲介，才能順利借精生子，用自己的子宮生下自己的孩子。

那麼，當現實情況的性愛、生育，都已逐漸和婚姻價值脫鉤時，仍以（異性戀）婚姻關係綁定性的權利、生育的權利、決定自己的子宮的權利，我們為什麼還需要用婚姻關係定義情感價值的存續？

回到電影開頭，杜夫在生育話題第一次被中斷，但還是想和小詩發生性關係後，他接著又要延續話題、卻再次被拒絕時，他為什麼不想繼續做愛了？如果不是以生育為性愛的目的，如果性愛僅僅只是性與愛的話，為什麼看到保險套就不做了？

那些真正橫亙在戀人之間的，關於人的組成差異，透過三個角色各自的困境，各自展現出關於愛的不同面向，都有著相通的任性、嫉妒與恐懼。藉由三人之間截然不同的性格，關係也在每一場戲裡來回流轉，廣瀨奈奈子細膩地刻劃人物的情感，卻也避免了太過濫情地訴諸於角色各自的背景。

不過在電影的結尾，的確會令部分觀眾感到失望，某些段落的戲劇呈現確實過分理想，但這也不礙於電影整體的表現。

尤其是周旋在兩個戀人之間的小詩，她所創作的兒童繪本角色「香菇小姐」，在他人眼裡看來是陰鬱的成人文學，潤奈更認為香菇小姐就是小詩的投射，而杜夫則始終不解小詩與原生家庭的疏遠之因。

《事到如今還談什麼愛》電影劇照／劇照提供：台北金馬影展執行委員會

直到三人正式達成共同養育孩子的決定，接著要討論該由誰提供卵子、子宮時，我們才透過小詩輕巧帶過的幾句話，而片面地理解了小詩排斥生小孩的原因。

小詩筆下的人物的確是她自己，但是她為什麼會成為現在的自己，在電影裡並不是那麼重要。這個意思是，「任性、狡猾、可愛且迷人」的性格，未必需要深究其成長背景、創傷經驗，它也可以僅僅作為一個人與生俱來的特質。

同樣地，杜夫的溫柔、體貼入微，也不一定需要冠上「女性特質」的標籤，而潤奈相對冷漠、疏離的性格，也只不過是另外一種組成而已。

在關係裡的不同組成，有時候我們不也將它稱之為「火花」嗎？

《釀電影》，「如果月亮背面是汪洋，日光就是生命的海流──金馬 63 專題」主視覺。／圖像提供：釀電影（設計：林雅萱）

月亮是最古早的電視，而電影百年的靈光， 是被迫倒下的巨樹身後，有眾人為祂記憶。

如果月亮背面是汪洋， 日光就是生命的海流。

article_text:
Cine

Godzilla Minus Zero – Crítica de la película

Gerardo Frías

Al igual que la entrega pasada, Godzilla Minus Zero apuesta por una trama social y geopolítica... pero se queda corta.

En 2023, Godzilla Minus One tomó por sorpresa al mundo: con un presupuesto de menos de 15 millones de dólares, Takashi Yamazaki se llevó el Óscar a Mejores efectos visuales y convirtió al rey de los monstruos en el reflejo de las cicatrices de posguerra de Japón. Tres años después, Yamazaki regresa como director, guionista y supervisor de efectos con Godzilla Minus Zero , una secuela directa ambientada en 1949 , dos años después de los hechos de la primera, que retoma a la familia Shikishima, de nuevo con Ryunosuke Kamiki y Minami Hamabe, frente a una nueva calamidad. Esta vez, además, con la llegada de King Ghidorah.

Entiendo que estas versiones de Godzilla, Minus One y Minus Zero , apuestan por una trama social y geopolítica de fondo más que por los monstruos en sí, y es una propuesta válida. El problema es que la trama humana debería ser igual de importante que el espectáculo: el contexto de la película gira en torno a Godzilla, y todo lo demás es consecuencia de nuestras pobres decisiones y batallas como humanidad. Pero aquí esa trama se siente lenta, repetitiva y, a pesar de que se toman todo el tiempo del mundo para explorarla, termina quedando corta.

Los ejemplos sobran. Vemos los motivos del odio a Estados Unidos por parte del profesor, pero esa trama y esas emociones no llegan a nada: si bien nos regalan una secuencia visual impactante a más no poder, se termina por resolver con un simple cambio de opinión. La conspiración de Estados Unidos, que pudo explorarse muchísimo más, termina sin llegar a ningún lado a mi parecer. El personaje del piloto, que tuvo una gran participación en la película pasada, queda sobreexplotado y su interacción se siente algo forzada. Y Noriko, afectada por Godzilla desde la cinta anterior, pudo tener mucho más desarrollo, pero se reduce a algo que hemos visto mil veces: el cómo hacer que Godzilla aparezca, y hasta ahí.

Tampoco ayuda que los grandes efectos especiales queden algo desaprovechados. De la cantidad de minutos que dura la película, vemos a Godzilla apenas una pequeña fracción del tiempo, entiendo que Ghidorah aparece muchísimo más, sin embargo me quedo con ganas de más Godzilla y sobre todo de una mejor batalla.

Y eso que la película tiene muchas cosas buenas: un fantástico diseño de arte, fotografía, efectos especiales y actuaciones. Pero se queda corta en ritmo y desarrollo para el tiempo que ocupa en pantalla, y me deja con la sensación de haber querido ver más de unas cosas y de pensar en muchas otras que pudieron saltarse durante la trama.

Es una gran película para hablar y pensar en política de época, sociedad y la complejidad emocional humana. Pero, hasta cierto punto, creo que Godzilla sale sobrando en la trama y faltando muchísimo en lo visual. En lo muy personal yo disfrutaría mil veces más una película de Godzilla del MonsterVerse de Legendary, pero eso tiene que ver con lo que yo espero al ir a ver una película de Godzilla. Sin embargo, estoy seguro de que muchos la disfrutaran, así que dense la oportunidad de juzgarla y disfrutarla ustedes, pues al final es un gran trabajo el que lleva detrás esta película.

Gerardo Frías

article_text:
現代童画会の公募展が11月10日、東京都美術館で始まりました。 １階の第１～第３展示室を使って、多種多様な作品 合計482点が一堂に並びます。

第52回 現代童画展

会場：東京都美術館（東京都台東区上野公園8-36）

会期：2026年11月10日(月)～11月15日(日)

休館日：期間中なし

開館時間：午前９時30分～午後５時30分。最終日の入場は午後２時まで

入場料：大人 600円。大学生以下 ・障害者手帳をお持ちの方、および付添者2名まで ・パスポート明示の方（日本人含む）は入場無料

詳しくは 現代童画会HP

現代童画会は、素朴派などと訳される「ナイーブ・アート」の新しいスタイル確立を目指して、1975年に結成されました。画家のほか、絵本作家やイラストレーター、デザイナーらも幅広く参加。会名の「童画」には、子供のような純粋な心でキャンバスに表現するという想いが込められています。

最高賞の「現代童画大賞」に選ばれたのは、宮沢寛之さんの《渦、そして舞い戻る。》、《夜、そして舞い踊る。》です。宮沢さんは、これまでも鳥を描いてきました。今回の作品も、夜の渋谷スクランブル交差点で踊るカラスと、自然へと帰っていくカラスを描きました。点描部分は10色以上のポスカを使っています。宮沢さんは「鳥は人間のメタファーです」と説明します。

「会員作家賞」は、今回初めて２作品が選ばれました。東野穂澄さんの《そよ風の音色》、《サンセットドリーム》と、横井佑次さんの《ハロウィンナイトⅠ》、《ハロウィンナイトⅡ》、《ハロウィンナイトⅢ》です。

横井さんは、アクリル板の裏一面を黒で塗りつぶし、黒色を削った部分に色を入れていく「バックドローイングアート」という独自の技法を追求しています。「表面の光沢や、色の鮮やかさは写真では分からないので、実際に見てください」と来場を呼びかけます。

会友作家賞は、茂手木聡子さんの《Eternal Voyage》。海底に沈んだ船を幻想的に描きました。

一般公募の頂点となる「現代童画会賞」は、ベルギー出身のロワゾー・ルンさんの《The Dreamers》が受賞しました。現在、山梨県の南アルプスの大自然の中に住み、 森や自然との深いつながりからインスピレーションを得て、 森が私たちに与えてくれる慈しみや優しさを描いています。

受賞作品以外では、洗練された線で描かれた独特な女性像で注目が高まっている若手日本画家、 丁子紅子 さんが162.1cm×260.6cmの大作《夜（よ）を脱ぐ。》を出展。「サナギが今まで まとっていたものから羽化するイメージで描きました」という作品は、見る人に希望を感じさせます。

小澤清人会長は、人形に花を合わせた《虞美人草》、《山百合》、《薔薇》、《曼珠沙華》の４点組で、新たなテーマへの挑戦を示しました。

ほかにも幻想的なものから写実的なものまで、とても幅広い作品が500点近く集まっていますので、自分の「推し」を見つけて、今後の活動に注目してみてはいかがでしょうか。 （美術展ナビ編集班・若水浩）

article_text:
I f only Angelina Jolie’s latest directorial effort, Without Blood, could be as pointed and consequential as her words in real life. If only the film, about the human toll of war, could draw blood as she does.

Jolie, a film-maker and former UN ambassador, has long been an outspoken advocate and humanitarian. She was also one of the first and remains among the few Hollywood stars to speak up for Palestinian lives, criticizing the lack of humanitarian aid provided to innocent civilians.

She’s made films in the past about the Bosnian war (In the Land of Blood and Honey) and the Cambodian civil war (First They Killed My Father). But in Without Blood, she wrestles with Alessandro Baricco’s stubbornly vague novel about the lingering traumas from an unspecified conflict.

Baricco’s text, about a man and a woman linked across time by brutal act of violence, resists any association with identifiable conflicts. That’s its ploy for universality, a faux generous and frankly overrated gesture. Sure, it worked for Incendies, the film that Without Blood most resembles. But Incendies gained more notice for director Denis Villeneuve’s deft hand with narrative craftsmanship, atmosphere and tension than the story it was telling. And if the recent wave of more diverse storytellers has taught us anything, it’s that specificity helps anchor narratives in a human experience that feels authentic, and universal by default.

Without Blood instead leaves its mismatched stars, Salma Hayek Pinault and Demián Bichir, flailing with words, anecdotes and frustratingly tedious and abstract conversations that feel like they’re searching for meaning – beyond the obvious and didactic sentiment that war causes harm and solves nothing.

Hayek and Bichir (the latter faring slightly better with the hollow material) play Nina and Tito. We can only guess that they’re living in the mid-50s in Mexico, though that’s never stated. He’s the weary operator of a kiosk. She’s the mysterious woman exuding mischievous warmth. Nina flirtatiously insists Tito join her for a meal. He resists at first, before resigning himself to this fated confrontation with the woman he met as a child, when Tito was a young rebel with a hand in her family’s assassination.

The instigating scene is among the few affecting moments in Without Blood, because Jolie sits in the violence and lets its ugliness fester. The drawn-out standoff – where vengeful gunmen continue a cycle of violence while giving monologues that are too arch for the cast to deliver convincingly – is extremely western-flavoured. So is the virtuosic opening tracking shot when riders on horseback lasso a young man and drag him across the dirt. There’s a heaviness to the violence in these early moments, which the film struggles to sustain.

In the present, Nina and Tito take turns narrating their own stories to each other, with a sense that they know each other’s next move. And they occasionally lean on over-the-top gestures to land dramatic points. In one moment, Hayek slowly turns a porcelain cup 180 degrees by its handle as she underlines a revelation. She does so with such self-satisfaction it verges on parodic.

They unwrap the expansive narrative, where there are no clear-cut heroes or villains, mostly for the audience’s sake, detailing the cascading violence, sexual abuse, dehumanization and traumas since their last confrontation. Tito’s mostly haunted by what Nina has endured, the gender gap in how war is experienced, made explicit. Moments where Nina pegs Tito’s existence as a performance of normalcy, even when performing basic functions looking right to cross the street, transcend, even if the observation feels more written for the movies than life.

Without Blood trades in tropes, often knowingly. There’s the aforementioned western iconography along with touches from lavish spy thrillers or 50s melodramas. The film, like the novel, indulges in genre, maybe as a deconstruction of how these stories celebrate violence and heroism. Or maybe genre is just another refuge from the real world.

Jolie also lays it on thick stylistically, as if compensating for a hollowness at her lavish, sepia-toned film’s core. Without Blood is brimming with fussed-over images – from the sentimental slow-motion bits with golden light refracting against the lens, or the glistening wet cobble-stoned streets that Nina treads across in heels towards her mark.

Surprisingly, the film hits a powerful note in its final moment, where the ambiguity works in its favour. Jolie abandons the characters in a moment that’s both comforting and unsettling, where the sense of inevitability, which up to that moment dictated their lives, fades, and we have no clue what their intentions are and whether they know how to move forward.

Without Blood is screening at the Toronto film festival and will be released at a later date

article_text:
Source: Sara De Santis

Jeff Deutchman, Neon head of acquisitions, production and development

There are two ways Neon cuts through the noise of a crowded distribution landscape and talent needs to be aligned in order to achieve success, senior executive Jeff Deutchman has told an industry audience.

“The key to maintaining our business in a way that can sustain is through a couple of different transformations,” the company’s head of acquisitions, production and development said. “One is cost sensitivity and the other is eventising everything that we do.”

Deutchman continued, “Movies probably can’t cost what they used to, especially if it’s important to us to take creative risks and have a robust theatrical release. And it’s important for talent, especially the highest-paid talent, to get on board with that.”

Speaking in his first trip to Brazil at the sixth Audiovisual Ideas Market, the business arm of the 50th São Paulo International Film Festival known as Mostra de São Paulo, Deutchman said there must still be a compelling reason for people to go to the cinema.

“That can be spectacle, quality, originality or representation,” he said. “But it has to be something.”

He added, “If there’s a crisis, as I understand it, it would be that film is no longer the only dominant popular art form. We have to share eyeballs with many other media and art. But the good news is there is evidence that it’s only going to erode the film business by so much, because the actual movie-going is thriving right now.”

The allure of ‘The Secret Agent’

Deutchman used Kleber Mendonça Filho’s Oscar-nominated The Secret Agent (2025) to illustrate Neon’s interest in Brazilian storytelling. “I remember my first thoughts, especially through the first two-thirds of the film: I felt like I was watching the best American studio thriller since Michael Clayton [2007], despite not being an American studio film. It’s very Brazilian, but it feels still better than anything the studios have produced in a very long time.”

Because the film could be marketed as a thriller, Deutchman “knew’’ it would get great reviews and work well for a US audience. Out of the $22m-plus at the worldwide box office, $4.3m came from North America. The Secret Agent earned four Oscar nominations for best picture, international feature film, lead actor for Wagner Moura, and casting.

“Kleber understands the language of classic Hollywood cinema so well and uses it so expertly. But then he also pulls the rug out and upends a lot of the expectations”, added Deutchman. There had been speculation that Neon might acquire Brazil’s current Oscar submission, Allan Deberton’s Gugu’s World, however despite a meeting with the film team in São Paulo, it is understood there has been no deal.

In terms of Neon’s overall success, Deutchman attributes it “to having dexterity to handle all different-size movies”. The company’s track record includes seven consecutive Cannes Palme d’Or winners, most recently Fjord earlier this year.

“When you’re an independent film company, you can’t afford to be too specific,’’ Deutchman said, adding that flexibility has allowed Neon to be “more imaginative”. He added, “We might buy a film because it feels like a good arthouse title. But as we get closer to release, we might see that there’s an opportunity to do something bigger with it.”

What has not changed since the company was founded in 2017 is “the underdog mentality and the entrepreneurial spirit”. “When you limit the risks that you can take, you miss things. And audiences frequently want something new, such as Parasite [2019] or Longlegs [2024],” the executive added.

Neon set out to disprove the fallacy that there was a ceiling on how well international films could perform in the US. “The only way to do that was to take the risk of treating these films the same way we would treat any English-language film on our slate in terms of spending,” he said.

The first film where Neon adopted this strategy was Ali Abbasi’s Border in 2018. “But it didn’t work, despite being an amazing film. The second one we did it with was Parasite ,” he recalled, referencing Bong Joon Ho’s $250m global box-office hit that became the first non-English language film to win best picture at the 2020 Oscars.

However he advised with a laugh that it was crucial not to draw the wrong conclusion from that film’s historic achievement. “When Parasite was a hit, we didn’t say to ourselves, ‘We have to go find a new Korean Hitchcockian thriller.’ That is the solution.”

Mostra de São Paulo closes on October 29.

title_original: Paweł Pawlikowski on Fatherland, Watching Sandra Hüller Act, and Going Against the Grain of Modern Filmmaking
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "When Thomas Mann visited post-war Germany in 1949, he was perhaps the most famous living German author. More than that, Mann was an exemplar of a “good German,” someone who had disavowed the Nazi government, was stripped of his citizenship, and forced into exile."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Mann (Hanns Zischler) tours the ruins of a partitioned country with his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller). Their journey from Frankfurt to Weimar captures the range of German society, from Nazi collaborators to political prisoners, from the wealthy to the dispossessed."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Mann tries to frame his journey within the works of Goethe, in part because he has been given an award dedicated to the writer. Hüller’s Erika, on the other hand, is grieving over the suicide of her brother Klaus (August Diehl), her closest confidant."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I spoke with Pawlikowski on Fatherland ‘s opening weekend in New York."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Film Stage: What struck me about Fatherland is its overwhelming grief. The layers of grief that Erika faces with her brother Klaus, that Thomas Mann faces returning to a ruined country, the grief of coping with the Allies and Russia."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paweł Pawlikowski : It depends on who watches it, I suppose. When you make a slightly understated film, it depends on who’s watching it as to what they get out of it. That’s the purpose of making films which don’t advertise broadly what they’re doing, which is the norm these days. Filmmakers will just tell you what you’re supposed to be feeling and thinking all the time."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Back to your question, yeah, it’s largely about grief. And how would you cope with grief? How do you go on with life when somebody’s committed suicide? How do you cope with the loss of your country?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You credit Colm Tóibín in the credits."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was just a gesture because a producer sent me his book [ The Magician ] to possibly adapt into a biopic or TV series. Mann’s life, it’s a huge story. I just picked one episode from it, one that is not actually from the book. But I wanted to make a gesture towards Colm who is a great writer."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Are they Mann’s actual speeches? Did you adapt them?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "No, they are Mann’s speeches. In fact, one of them is recorded. You can find it in the Hessischen Rundfunks, the German sound archives. They are also printed. I used two original speeches, but I also conflated the first one with another speech Mann made called Über Demokratie , About Democracy . The quote from Clemenceau about the German romantic cult of death wasn’t in the Frankfurt speech. I added it because it kind of made sense in the story."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Pawlikowski.-Copyright_-Aleksandra-Modrzejewska-Mitan-1-960x1200.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Photo courtesy of Aleksandra Modrzejewska."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What drew you to Thomas Mann to begin with?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I like some of his books very much. He’s not my favorite, the passionate love of my life. I wouldn’t put his portrait above my desk, you know. But I’ve always liked his shorter stories and things like The Magic Mountain . The reason I did this was that trip in 1949. It’s an imagined fictional story using real people, perhaps slightly irresponsibly. If it works, it works. If it doesn’t, then everyone will blame me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It wasn’t so much Thomas Mann, in fact. I was interested in that triangle of Mann and Erika and Klaus. I was interested in the story of the most famous German writer alive at the time, coming back to his country after 16 years in exile. And the country has changed beyond recognition. It’s in ruins. A country that turned its back on him."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I loved that situation. And the question, “Where is home?” So I was just freely using Mann’s biography to tell an intimate, personal story. There are so many stories you could draw from the Mann family. There are so many points of departure. Maybe I should start an industry of making films out of fragments of the Mann family. I would never tackle the whole story, this huge philosophical soap opera that was the Mann family, you know?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But people ask me, “Are you interested in Thomas Mann?” Yes, relatively. But I was more interested in this moment, and in these three characters entangled together. It’s the makings of a Greek tragedy: the brother and sister, the daughter and father, the father and son. It’s just so rich. You don’t need any more. And fused with the historical factor, it gives me something very powerful. Which I do everything in my means to downplay in my typical style."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Can you talk about working with your performers? Hüller has a scene where she slaps Gründgens at a bar that seems completely spur-of-the-moment. How do you work with her to achieve that?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "That was a pretty precise scene, a pretty precisely written one. I fiddled with it a bit; the slap came at the right time. I even timed it with the music in the background, so they could work together."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Some scenes are really tightly written. Others, I kind of massage into place, just before shooting, or even while shooting. I have the luxury of editing as I shoot. We shoot for five days and take a day off to relax. Then one day to put the footage together. There’s not too much editing because there’s not much coverage. I put the building blocks and the film starts emerging for me, like some kind of documentary."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Every actor is different. Every actor has a different process. Sandra is a phenomenal actress who has her own needs, her own process. She has to work from within all the time. There’s nothing mechanical about her acting, nothing technical. I mean, she has technique like nobody else I’ve met, but it has to come out from inside her. She has to plug into it in her own way."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I kind of limited her acting by not doing coverage. Not having the camera catch her work, you know? Our shots are very set, very precise. She has to be brilliant within the shot, the frame. That can be difficult, but it’s also the beauty of this kind of filmmaking. She took to it really well after a while. First, she was a bit surprised, but then she really kind of understood that the image and the performance come together to kind of enhance each other."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was fascinating watching her. There would be one take in those important scenes where you got goosebumps. The slap with Gründgens, there is this wonderful moment where her face changes while he’s saying these insulting things. Insulting and relatively true as well. That’s why she slaps him, because he’s saying, “It’s easy for you not to sell your soul, you’re a nepo baby, you got it easy. Money, languages, contacts, your father.” What happens in her face is just mind-blowing. There’s always one magical take where it seems to just happen somehow."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Fatherland-Behind-the-Scenes-1200x900.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "What’s really challenging is that she’s not allowed to show her emotions in public."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She does blow her fuse, twice, actually. But the drama in her face is unbelievable. That’s what makes the film for me. It’s like, “Wow, what’s happening there?”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A lot of performance you can get from the context of the shot. It’s not just about what the actor does, but how you hold the shot, where the shot comes from. You kind of know what they’re feeling, even if they’re not showing it. Hans Zischler really underplays Thomas Mann, but you get what he’s feeling without him having to do much. Maybe like a flick of the eyebrow tells you so much. The little twinkle in his eye, or tiny gestures. The context gives them meaning."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It’s a bit suicidal these days to do that because in cinema now everything’s big and noisy and underlined and music tells you what to think and actors are acting away furiously. It’s going against the grain somewhat. It clearly will divide the audience."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How hard was it to recreate the era?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was time-consuming. We spent a lot of time looking for locations in Lower Silesia, an area of Poland that belonged to Germany before the Second World War. article_text:
When Thomas Mann visited post-war Germany in 1949, he was perhaps the most famous living German author. More than that, Mann was an exemplar of a “good German,” someone who had disavowed the Nazi government, was stripped of his citizenship, and forced into exile.

In Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , Mann (Hanns Zischler) tours the ruins of a partitioned country with his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller). Their journey from Frankfurt to Weimar captures the range of German society, from Nazi collaborators to political prisoners, from the wealthy to the dispossessed.

Mann tries to frame his journey within the works of Goethe, in part because he has been given an award dedicated to the writer. Hüller’s Erika, on the other hand, is grieving over the suicide of her brother Klaus (August Diehl), her closest confidant.

I spoke with Pawlikowski on Fatherland ‘s opening weekend in New York.

The Film Stage: What struck me about Fatherland is its overwhelming grief. The layers of grief that Erika faces with her brother Klaus, that Thomas Mann faces returning to a ruined country, the grief of coping with the Allies and Russia.

Paweł Pawlikowski : It depends on who watches it, I suppose. When you make a slightly understated film, it depends on who’s watching it as to what they get out of it. That’s the purpose of making films which don’t advertise broadly what they’re doing, which is the norm these days. Filmmakers will just tell you what you’re supposed to be feeling and thinking all the time.

Back to your question, yeah, it’s largely about grief. And how would you cope with grief? How do you go on with life when somebody’s committed suicide? How do you cope with the loss of your country?

You credit Colm Tóibín in the credits.

It was just a gesture because a producer sent me his book [ The Magician ] to possibly adapt into a biopic or TV series. Mann’s life, it’s a huge story. I just picked one episode from it, one that is not actually from the book. But I wanted to make a gesture towards Colm who is a great writer.

Are they Mann’s actual speeches? Did you adapt them?

No, they are Mann’s speeches. In fact, one of them is recorded. You can find it in the Hessischen Rundfunks, the German sound archives. They are also printed. I used two original speeches, but I also conflated the first one with another speech Mann made called Über Demokratie , About Democracy . The quote from Clemenceau about the German romantic cult of death wasn’t in the Frankfurt speech. I added it because it kind of made sense in the story.

Photo courtesy of Aleksandra Modrzejewska.

What drew you to Thomas Mann to begin with?

I like some of his books very much. He’s not my favorite, the passionate love of my life. I wouldn’t put his portrait above my desk, you know. But I’ve always liked his shorter stories and things like The Magic Mountain . The reason I did this was that trip in 1949. It’s an imagined fictional story using real people, perhaps slightly irresponsibly. If it works, it works. If it doesn’t, then everyone will blame me.

It wasn’t so much Thomas Mann, in fact. I was interested in that triangle of Mann and Erika and Klaus. I was interested in the story of the most famous German writer alive at the time, coming back to his country after 16 years in exile. And the country has changed beyond recognition. It’s in ruins. A country that turned its back on him.

I loved that situation. And the question, “Where is home?” So I was just freely using Mann’s biography to tell an intimate, personal story. There are so many stories you could draw from the Mann family. There are so many points of departure. Maybe I should start an industry of making films out of fragments of the Mann family. I would never tackle the whole story, this huge philosophical soap opera that was the Mann family, you know?

But people ask me, “Are you interested in Thomas Mann?” Yes, relatively. But I was more interested in this moment, and in these three characters entangled together. It’s the makings of a Greek tragedy: the brother and sister, the daughter and father, the father and son. It’s just so rich. You don’t need any more. And fused with the historical factor, it gives me something very powerful. Which I do everything in my means to downplay in my typical style.

Can you talk about working with your performers? Hüller has a scene where she slaps Gründgens at a bar that seems completely spur-of-the-moment. How do you work with her to achieve that?

That was a pretty precise scene, a pretty precisely written one. I fiddled with it a bit; the slap came at the right time. I even timed it with the music in the background, so they could work together.

Some scenes are really tightly written. Others, I kind of massage into place, just before shooting, or even while shooting. I have the luxury of editing as I shoot. We shoot for five days and take a day off to relax. Then one day to put the footage together. There’s not too much editing because there’s not much coverage. I put the building blocks and the film starts emerging for me, like some kind of documentary.

Every actor is different. Every actor has a different process. Sandra is a phenomenal actress who has her own needs, her own process. She has to work from within all the time. There’s nothing mechanical about her acting, nothing technical. I mean, she has technique like nobody else I’ve met, but it has to come out from inside her. She has to plug into it in her own way.

I kind of limited her acting by not doing coverage. Not having the camera catch her work, you know? Our shots are very set, very precise. She has to be brilliant within the shot, the frame. That can be difficult, but it’s also the beauty of this kind of filmmaking. She took to it really well after a while. First, she was a bit surprised, but then she really kind of understood that the image and the performance come together to kind of enhance each other.

It was fascinating watching her. There would be one take in those important scenes where you got goosebumps. The slap with Gründgens, there is this wonderful moment where her face changes while he’s saying these insulting things. Insulting and relatively true as well. That’s why she slaps him, because he’s saying, “It’s easy for you not to sell your soul, you’re a nepo baby, you got it easy. Money, languages, contacts, your father.” What happens in her face is just mind-blowing. There’s always one magical take where it seems to just happen somehow.

What’s really challenging is that she’s not allowed to show her emotions in public.

She does blow her fuse, twice, actually. But the drama in her face is unbelievable. That’s what makes the film for me. It’s like, “Wow, what’s happening there?”

A lot of performance you can get from the context of the shot. It’s not just about what the actor does, but how you hold the shot, where the shot comes from. You kind of know what they’re feeling, even if they’re not showing it. Hans Zischler really underplays Thomas Mann, but you get what he’s feeling without him having to do much. Maybe like a flick of the eyebrow tells you so much. The little twinkle in his eye, or tiny gestures. The context gives them meaning.

It’s a bit suicidal these days to do that because in cinema now everything’s big and noisy and underlined and music tells you what to think and actors are acting away furiously. It’s going against the grain somewhat. It clearly will divide the audience.

How hard was it to recreate the era?

It was time-consuming. We spent a lot of time looking for locations in Lower Silesia, an area of Poland that belonged to Germany before the Second World War. We spent a lot of time with my production designers Marcel Sławiński and Katarzyna Sobańska and with my DP Łukasz Żal driving around, taking photographs, identifying what we could kind of piece together and make a world out of. Time-consuming but very satisfying in the end. In the beginning, I had misgivings that we could actually do it.

The trick is to find really good extras. We spent five months looking for extras in every location where we were shooting. My assistants looked for good faces, faces from the period who don’t look like people today. That helps authenticate the period as well.

I don’t know how you got those opening shots in Frankfurt, following a motorcycle down block after block of wreckage.

It’s a long street in Legnica in Silesia. It used to be Liegnitz in German. A very down-at-the-heels area, poor, impoverished, run-down. It looked pretty damaged, then we added our own rubble. Our production design had this kind of three-dimensional rubble, and then above eye level we added some digital effects. We had about 600 meters of good street, and then the extras were great. It was a painstaking job to create that.

I loved the nightclub scene, a very de-glamorized version of what would appear in an MGM film. The lighting is flatter; you’re often shooting at floor level to show these shuffling dancers. It’s something that would have really existed.

It’s like good photo reportage from era. That was our point of reference: journalist photography from the period. Cartier-Bresson. Not glossy and not ornamental.

Talking about collaborating with your DP Łukasz Żal, how do you build those spectacular frames?

We set up the shots together. I’m kind of more into framing. He’s more involved with lighting, but actually we’re symbiotic. So you can’t tell where the border is.

The film is based around the image. The mise-en-scène serves the image rather than having the camera covering the scene in a traditional way. Building the image is a crucial component. We started working that way on Ida . We don’t need to talk too much, we just kind of prepare it together.

Having said that, the production designers Marcel and Katarzyna are very closely involved from quite early on in the process. Like Łukasz, they also worked on Ida and Cold War .

So it’s not just the DP coming and making shots. It’s more like building the film with the help of the DP and the production designers. People say photography, it’s actually about the image, image-making. How do you frame? What faces are in the shot? What’s the relationship between foreground and background? What’s in focus?

Also, how long you hold onto a shot. You take an editing credit on Fatherland . Had you done that before?

No, I never took a credit, but I’m very involved in editing. I’m always in the cutting room making decisions. On this one I had this young editor [Piotr Wójcik] who was just supposed to press buttons, because I hate all the digital stuff. But he ended up being very good. So he got a credit as well.

I love editing, and, like I said, I edit as I’m shooting. Every five days, I look at the cut and see what the film is more clearly. I kind of forget about the script, and just see how this documentary that I’m making is coming along.

Is it faster to shoot without coverage?

Yes, but to get the shot right takes a bit of time. We have to reframe sometimes. Then I try to combine the background action with extras with the foreground. It’s a bit more fiddly in that way, but at least you don’t have to move the lights around many times.

What must have been frustrating for Mann was that he didn’t have any choices between “Mickey Mouse and Stalin,” as Klaus put it. Mann’s looking for a way to restore his country to what Goethe imagined, but he has no good path.

He got to the limits of politics. In the end, the good thing about being a great artist is that he can always write books. He can move to Switzerland, where everyone goes if they don’t know where they go or where they belong. That is if they have enough money.

Politically, he was hoping to unify on the basis of this humanist culture. It’s clearly not working. His way of thinking, his language, are at odds with the language of the time, with the simple narratives that are being pushed on both sides. So, yeah, there’s no political way out.

Mann realizes, together with Erica and Klaus, that they’ve lost their fatherland, their homeland. Which a lot of people face today. So the film has its kind of contemporary resonance.

Your film still shows, through Mozart and Bach, through architecture and landscapes, that there is a Germany worth remembering for Mann.

Part of that Germany is in his books. He was such a German writer. He famously said, “Where I am, that’s where German culture is.” A bit over the top, but when you think about it, Germany did exist in culture above all its divisions. There is a continuum. Of course, the country itself was destroyed and polarized, like the world is today. But we can hope that culture is still above that. I mean, even today there’s hope, right?

Fatherland is now in theaters.

article_text:
「KIRIKANE Sculpture 山本茜」がそごう美術館（横浜）で12月6日まで開催されています。日本の伝統工芸「截金（きりかね）」とガラスを組み合わせた「截金ガラス」という独自の表現で注目を集める山本茜さんの、美術館では初の個展です。

グッズ売り場も見逃せません。ポストカードやカレンダー、クリアファイルなどのアイテムから、唯一無二の美の世界を身近に感じることができます。山本さんがライフワークとして取り組み続けてきた「源氏物語シリーズ」を中心に、いくつか購入しましたので、紹介しましょう。

ポストカード 各200円

特に充実していたのがポストカードです。本展で初公開の最新作《源氏物語シリーズ第十八帖「松風」―浮木舟―》はもちろん、展示されていた「源氏物語シリーズ」全種類がそろっていました（品切れの場合もあります）。

「玉の男御子」のまばゆさが鮮烈な第一帖「桐壺」をはじめ、第四十帖「御法」、第四十五帖「橋姫」など、特に印象的だった作品のポストカードを購入。 なかでも第十九帖「薄雲」―雪明り― のポストカードは、作品を上から見たときに現れる、幻想的な情景を留めた一枚です。もう一度会場で、同じ角度から作品を味わいたくなりました。

クリアファイル 450円

《源氏物語シリーズ第三帖「空蟬」》 のクリアファイルです。空蝉が残した薄衣。その文様を思わせる、繊細な截金をじっくりと見ることができます。いつまでも眺めていられそうですね。

デスクカレンダー 1,150円

今の季節にぜひ購入したいカレンダー。こちらも源氏物語シリーズで構成されています。

ショップでは、「源氏物語シリーズ」以外の作品のグッズも販売されていました。お気に入りの作品のグッズがあるか、ぜひ探してみてください。

（読売新聞美術展ナビ編集班・美間実沙 撮影・吉成）

article_text:
“ Gintama : Yoshiwara in Flames” – the latest iteration of the “Gintama” story – previewed this week at Lucca Comics and Games, Europe’s largest Comic-Con, prior to a theatrical release in Italy. Variety spoke with director Naoya Andô and producer Ryo Nakamuray about their continuation of the saga.

“Gintama” started life as a manga, authored and drawn by Hideaki Sorachi. Set in an alternative, sci-fi version of late-Edo-period Tokyo, the Earth has been invaded by the Amanto, an alien species, and three friends set off on a personal mission.

Related Stories

Italian Content Investment Dropped 7.4% in 2025 Largely Due to Uncertainty Over Domestic Tax Credits, Rome MIA Market Report Says

'Beast in Me' Season 2 Casts John Goodman

The manga became a long-running 367-episode anime series and has had three previous big-screen spin-offs. “Gintama: Yoshiwara in Flames” is the fourth cinema outing for the series.

How did you want to approach this franchise without losing its soul but at the same time making it suitably cinematic? Naoya Andô: When we started planning this film, we already knew that there would be many action scenes. We were keen to use the CinemaScope ultrawide ratio as well as using 3D in order to be able to move the camera more, and give us more variety, as well as keep the camera a little distant from the subjects so we could frame the shots better and really appreciate the design and setting. It’s for this reason we made this choice.

This story was already told in the TV series but despite the title Yoshiwara didn’t burn. But here we see it burn really. Naoya Andô: Our producer Takashi Maekawa also worked on the television series and so I asked him, are we going to actually burn the town this time? And the producer said: “Yes this time we’re going to burn everything.” And so we had talked among ourselves about how we were going to do it and the group made a creative decision to do it.

How important is Lucca Comic and Games for you to reach European fans and markets? Naoya Andô: Obviously, I am very honored and happy to have been invited to such an important event as Lucca. Up til now, we haven’t brought the films to Europe. This time we decided to try and bring the film here. Yesterday, we saw how the Italian fans of “Gintama” love the series and we were very happy to see the warmth of the reception we got.

Returning to such a well-loved narrative arc as “Yoshiwara in Flames,” how did you deal with the high expectations that audiences would have? Ryo Nakamuray: As you say, even in the original manga, this arc was hugely popular as well as the anime, but we felt there was enough time and we had the benefit of working on a different scale as well.

How do you transfer from television to the big screen? Naoya Andô: Obviously we tried to find aspects that were big and impressive both in the audio and visual aspects. But we finished the anime five years prior to beginning the film and in these five years, the technology has made great leaps forward. So we wanted to use these new technologies to push the film in new directions, especially using the 3D in the animation. We also worked on the music as well. There is a lot of new music.

There was a version of the film released earlier this year in Japan and then a new version released in September with over a hundred changed shots. What was behind this decision? Naoya Andô: We released the version in February because we had a deadline to respect and the film was finished and ready to be released, but we also knew that there were shots which weren’t perfect and could be improved and so when we had the opportunity we went back and perfected them. We were very proud of the film we released in February but with the opportunity of the DVD release we decided to go back and work again on the film and we retouched over 200 shots.

In the end titles there are tens of studios which appear from China to Indonesia to Vietnam. How do you coordinate so many teams? Ryo Nakamuray: In animation, you’re always dividing elements into teams. Some will be experts in character, over action scenes, etc., so we are always choosing the collaborators and animators who will be best for each element and so we’re always meeting up with these different studios and groups. Every group will have a team leader who is responsible for their work.

The film also has quite a lot of humor and meta-humor. Naoya Andô: Humor is very difficult to do and especially to translate culturally. It’s very, very difficult to do. We had one director who worked principally on that. What we figured out was that it was best not to present the humor to the audience as this bit is really funny, but rather have the characters themselves joke between themselves and the audience could listen in and enjoy the humor.

article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: NewFilmmakers Los Angeles has announced the lineup for its 2026 DocuSlate Documentary Film Festival, NFMLA ’s annual cinematic showcase of “stories spanning continents, generations, and communities.”

The event running November 12-15 opens with the North American premiere of Sergio & Mirta, A Love Story in 8 mm , directed by Fabrizio Laurenti and co-written and produced by Niccolò Vivarelli. “Constructed from rediscovered archival footage, the film offers an intimate window into the lives of Italian cult cinema director Sergio Corbucci and his then-wife Mirta Guarnaschelli,” notes a synopsis. “Capturing moments from their romance approximately 75 years ago, the documentary transforms personal images into a moving cinematic time capsule, preserving a little-seen chapter of film history.”

Related Stories

NewFilmmakers Los Angeles Announces Winners Of 14th NFMLA Awards; Nani Sahra Walker Claims Best New Filmmaker Prize

New Filmmakers Los Angeles To Screen Honey Lauren's Intersex-Themed 'Mistake' For Pride Month

The DocuSlate festival lineup spans seven film programs, highlighted by 12 documentary shorts and five documentary features, accompanied by filmmaker Q&A sessions, industry engagement opportunities, and two virtual panels. Sergio & Mirta, A Love Story in 8 mm is one of two North American premieres in a lineup that also includes one world premiere, one U.S. premiere, one West Coast premiere, and six Los Angeles premieres.

Watch on Deadline

Screenings begin Thursday, November 12, at Cinelounge Sunset Theater in Hollywood (located on the Hollywood Offices campus), continue Friday, November 13, and culminate in a full day of programming on Sunday, November 15, at South Park Center in Downtown Los Angeles.

Scroll for the complete list of 2026 DocuSlate films.

“This year’s selections offer an expansive portrait of the world through the perspectives of filmmakers working at the intersection of personal experience, cultural history, environmental change, political engagement, and community resilience,” states a news release. “Bringing together emerging filmmakers and established voices, the festival features work from Sundance, Tribeca, and SXSW alumni, alongside filmmakers whose collective accomplishments include four Emmy Award winners and two Emmy nominees. Among the selections is Ora DeKornfeld’s The Grandfather Puzzle , which earned Oscar-qualifying status after receiving Mountainfilm’s Best Short Documentary award.”

The 2026 edition highlights the continuing impact of NFMLA’s NewNarratives grant program, the arts and culture-focused nonprofit notes, with two projects connected to past and present grant recipients: The world premiere of Why Is Climate Changing? from 2026 NewNarratives Environmental Storytelling Grant recipient Lu Ren, and The Art of Sharing from 2025 NewNarratives grant recipients Jen and Ric Serena.

The festival concludes November 15 with the Los Angeles premiere of Uncommitted , directed by Razi Jafri and executive produced by W. Kamau Bell. “This investigative documentary examines the emergence, organizing efforts, and political impact of the Uncommitted National Movement, offering a timely exploration of grassroots activism, political participation, and the relationship between communities and institutions of power. With developments continuing to unfold, the film is expected to incorporate new updates following the November elections.”

Beyond the Screen: Connecting Filmmakers, Audiences, and Industry

In addition to its public screenings, DocuSlate 2026 will feature two virtual panel discussions and opportunities for participating filmmakers to engage with entertainment industry professionals, executives, and fellow creatives. These activities reflect NFMLA’s broader mission to help independent filmmakers build sustainable careers by connecting artistic talent with professional resources, industry relationships, and new audiences. Through its combination of film exhibitions, filmmaker conversations, and professional development opportunities, DocuSlate provides a space where documentary artists can share their work while contributing to a broader dialogue about the cultural and social significance of nonfiction cinema.

title_original: Rosana Paulino’s Pantheon of Black Plant Goddesses Arrives in Paris
editorial_title_zh: 罗萨娜·保利诺的黑人植物女神万神殿登陆巴黎
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这位艺术家在法国首都的门德斯·伍德画廊（Mendes Wood DM）举办了其正在进行中的“植物夫人”（Senhora das Plantas）系列展览。

Iansã）开始。“然后我把注意力转向了孪叶豆树（jatobá），”她补充道。该系列的作品很快出现在世界上历史最悠久的两个定期展览中：2022年和2026年的威尼斯双年展以及2023年的圣保罗双年展。在圣保罗，保利诺从纸本水彩转向了布面绘画，将她的素描放大到了近9英尺乘20英尺。接下来，她引入了红树林。这些画作中的女神带有宁静的气质，根基牢牢扎在大地中，同时还戴着随风摇曳的叶冠。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.375-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一幅由三联画构成的黑人女神红树林形象。", "caption": "罗萨娜·保利诺，《白鹭》，选自红树林系列，2023年。摄影：EstudioEmObra/鸣谢艺术家与圣保罗、布鲁塞尔、巴黎、纽约的门德斯·伍德画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "今年，她对“万年青”（Comigo Ninguém Pode，科学名称为 Lima）首次在门德斯·伍德画廊的纽约空间看到这些作品时，里面有“昼夜系列，罗萨娜在黑色背景下进行绘画和素描。我以前从未亲眼见过这些作品。它们传达出一种神秘感和魔法感；它们身上有一种真正打动我们的某种共鸣，”她谈到决定将该系列作品纳入威尼斯展出时说道。“而且它在意大利也产生了同样的影响。它是这个展览的巨大护身符，它被放置在入口处绝非偶然。”", "translated": true}, 《天使的号角》（Angel’s Trumpet），选自“植物夫人”系列，2026年。摄影：EstudioEmObra/鸣谢艺术家与圣保罗、布鲁塞尔、巴黎、纽约的门德斯·伍德画廊", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "随着她开始对那些在阴凉处生长或提供阴凉的物种（如“万年青”）产生兴趣，她的植物女神形象近期变得愈发扑朔迷离。保利诺对非裔巴西人宗教传统中用于精神保护的“力量植物”（plantas de poder）的研究也不断深入，她的植物与昼夜循环之间的关系变得更为广阔。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在巴黎，她将展示她所说的“夜间”画布，其中包含与曼陀罗属（Brugmansia）植物相关的新女神——或现有女神的新版本。这种植物以其色彩丰富（白色、橙红、紫色、丁香紫、粉色）的花朵而闻名，它们具有一种特殊的发光感，在某种意义上使花瓣看起来呈半透明状。它们迷人的特质掩盖了极端的毒性；它们有时被用作致幻剂，摄入后会导致严重的精神错乱甚至死亡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.600-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "一位带有凤梨科植物的黑人女神，背景为蓝色，背后有一个黄色圆圈。", "caption": "罗萨娜·保利诺，《无题》，选自“植物女士”系列，2026年。摄影：Gui Gomes/鸣谢艺术家及圣保罗、布鲁塞尔、巴黎、纽约的门德斯·伍德画廊（Mendes Wood DM）", "credit": "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "保利诺被这种二元性所吸引：“这是一种具有某种分量的植物——有体量、有气味。但它是现存最危险的植物之一。许多人在饮用了含有它的茶水后失去了生命。”在《天使的号角》（2026年）中，一个人物坐在地上，膝盖上垂下根须。她的眼中长出树枝，上面开着该植物的喇叭状花朵。在她的诱惑中，这位女神散发着力量。一件创作于2026年的无题作品则以一位凤梨科女神为主角，呈现出不同的氛围。坐着的人物呈瑜伽般的姿势扭转着躯干，叶子从她的口中涌出，仿佛她一直在滔滔不绝地说话。她的神情温和，留着短发，发质类似于紧密盘绕的卷发。保利诺使用她自己制作的一个工具实现了这种效果：一根前端粘有海绵的树枝。",
