The 16 paintings—five on paper and 12 on canvas—take on renewed vitality on a larger scale and via a deeper exploration of color and increasingly ingenious bodily poses."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The central question guiding Paulino’s work has long been “What is it like to be a Black woman in Brazil?” Active since the 1990s, she had seemingly answered it, until 2018, through an indictment of the enduring consequences of slavery in Brazilian society in works like Parede da Memória (Memory Wall, 1994), which engages with the extensive gaps in the family trees of Black Brazilian families, and Assentamento (Settlement, 2013), three photographs of an enslaved Black woman printed on fabric that she fragmented and stitched back together, adding a heart and a baby. Appropriated from images taken by Auguste Stahl and taken during the 1865–66 Thayer Expedition to Brazil, Paulino’s gesture aimed to restore the woman’s humanity and history from a set of photographs made to substantiate claims of racial degeneration supposedly caused by racial mixing."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At a 2018 retrospective at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, Paulino debuted a series of drawings from the early 2000s that anticipate the psychological exploration seen later in the goddesses of Senhora das Plantas .” Marked by restless lines, these works depict a woman tentatively emerging from a cocoon in a ritual of transformation and emancipation. “Drawing is a central foundation of Rosana’s practice; it sheds light on her imagination. Forms and ideas that she develops through drawing later acquire spatiality,” Valéria Piccoli, the exhibition’s cocurator, told ARTnews . “It was important to emphasize that she was the first voice in the 1990s to speak about the issue of Black women, but also to highlight that this was part of a much broader context of her interests and desires.”"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.598-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A painting with a blue ground of a nude Black woman who is connected to plants. ", "caption": "Rosana Paulino, Comigo ninguém pode, da série Senhora das Plantas | Comigo ninguém pode (Dumb Cane / “Don’t mess with me”) , from the “Lady of the Plants series,” 2026. Photo: Gui Gomes/Courtesy the artist and Mendes Wood DM, São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Less than a year later, she would show the earliest iteration of her botanical goddesses. A different sensibility had emerged: The figures, drawn in earth tones, were nude, but the hypersexualization of the Black female body was nowhere to be found. Instead, the works suggested a new way of conceiving wisdom and communion with nature. The series has its roots in the plants Paulino keeps in her studio. Before she named them goddesses, she initially called the plants in the series’ early works “folhas” (leaves)."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“I gradually realized that it couldn’t be that simple: plants have a history, so I began to approach them more specifically,” Paulino explained in a recent interview in her studio, noting that she began the series because she could find no Black goddesses in books devoted to the sacred feminine."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "She started first with snake plants ( Espada de Iansã in Portuguese). “Then I turned my attention to the jatobá tree,” she added. Works from the series soon appeared in the world’s two oldest recurring exhibitions: the 2022 and 2026 Venice Biennales and the 2023 Bienal de São Paulo. For São Paulo, Paulino moved from watercolor on paper to painting on canvas, scaling her drawings up to nearly 9 feet by 20 feet. Next, she introduced the mangrove. The goddesses in these paintings have a serene air, with roots firmly anchored in the earth, but also a crown of leaves that sway with the wind."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.375-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A three panel painting of a Black goddess as a mangrove. ", "caption": "Rosana Paulino, Garça branca, Da série mangue , 2023 Photo: EstudioEmObra/Courtesy the artist and Mendes Wood DM, São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "This year, her investigation into Comigo Ninguém Pode (scientifically known as Dieffenbachia ), a toxic plant also associated with spiritual protection, lend the Brazilian Pavilion its title. The pavilion’s curator Diane Lima first saw the works at Mendes Wood DM’s New York space, which had “the day and night series, in which Rosana paints and draws against a black background. I had never seen these works in person before. They convey a sense of mystery and magic; there is a certain aurality to them that truly moves us,” she said of her decision to include work form this series in Venice. “And it had that same impact in Italy. It is the exhibition’s great amulet, and it’s no coincidence that it is positioned right at the entrance.”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Approaching them as if she is still drawing at a table, Paulino lays flat her canvases, which she prepares with gesso mixture to seals the weave so they behave more like paper when she adds watercolor and acrylic on their surfaces. Her decision to work horizontally, however, also reflects a conceptual choice. “I’m not going to reproduce the watercolor brushstrokes on canvas. But at the same time, this idea of vertical painting is very Western. […] My thing is to work on a table,” she said."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.592-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A painting of a Black woman with angel's trumpets on a brown ground. ", "caption": "Rosana Paulino, Trombeta de Anjo, da série Senhora das Plantas | Angel’s Trumpet , from the “Lady of the Plants” series, 2026. Photo: EstudioEmObra/Courtesy the artist and Mendes Wood DM, São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Her plant goddesses have recently become more ambiguous as she has become interested in species that thrive in shade or offer it, like Comigo Ninguém Pode. And Paulino’s research into plantas de poder (plants of power), used for spiritual protection in Afro-Brazilian religious traditions, has only deepened, the relationship between her plants and the cycles of day and night becoming more expansive."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In Paris, she will show what she is calling “nocturnal” canvases featuring new goddesses—or new versions of existing ones—associated with angel’s trumpet ( Brugmansia ). A genus known for its exuberant flowers in a range of colors—white, salmon, purple, lilac, pink—they possess a particular luminosity that makes the petals seem, in a sense, translucent. Their alluring quality belies their extreme toxicity; at times used as a hallucinogen, their ingestion can cause severe mental confusion and even death."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.artnews.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/MW.ROP_.600-d0-hr.jpg?w=400", "alt": "A Black goddess with Bromeliaceae on a blue background with a yellow circle behind. ", "caption": "Rosana Paulino, Sem título, da série Senhora das Plantas | Untitled , from the “Lady of the Plants series,” 2026. Photo: Gui Gomes/Courtesy the artist and Mendes Wood DM, São Paulo, Brussels, Paris, New York", "credit": "ARTnews"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Paulino is drawn to this duality: “It’s a plant with a certain weight to it—a size, a scent. But it’s one of the most dangerous plants there is. Many people have lost their lives after ingesting teas containing it.” In Angel’s trumpet (2026), a figure sits on the ground, roots dangling from her knees. Branches emerge from her eyes, bearing the plant’s trumpet-shaped flowers. In her seduction, this goddess exudes strength. An untitled 2026 work, featuring a bromeliad goddess, inhabits a different atmosphere. The seated figure twists her torso in a yoga-like pose, while leaves emerge from her mouth as if she had been chattering animatedly. Her expression is gentle, and her hair cropped short, with a texture resembling tightly coiled hair. Paulino achieved this effect using a tool she made herself: a branch with a sponge attached to its tip."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“You don’t need long, flowing hair to be a goddess,” she said. “My series ‘Senhoras das Plantas’ exists because woman is an archetype that the West cannot fully comprehend,” the artist concludes."}]
article_text:
The growing visibility of Rosana Paulino ’s work reaches a new chapter with the opening this week of her first solo exhibition in Paris, at Mendes Wood DM ’s outpost in the French capital.

Titled “Bloom in the Sunlight, Dream in the Moonlight,” the exhibition introduces new plant goddesses into the Afro-botanical pantheon Paulino has been building since 2019 as part of her ongoing series “Senhora das Plantas” (Lady of the Plants), which elevates Black women to the status of goddesses in communion with nature, without implying a romanticized view. The 16 paintings—five on paper and 12 on canvas—take on renewed vitality on a larger scale and via a deeper exploration of color and increasingly ingenious bodily poses.

The central question guiding Paulino’s work has long been “What is it like to be a Black woman in Brazil?” Active since the 1990s, she had seemingly answered it, until 2018, through an indictment of the enduring consequences of slavery in Brazilian society in works like Parede da Memória (Memory Wall, 1994), which engages with the extensive gaps in the family trees of Black Brazilian families, and Assentamento (Settlement, 2013), three photographs of an enslaved Black woman printed on fabric that she fragmented and stitched back together, adding a heart and a baby. Appropriated from images taken by Auguste Stahl and taken during the 1865–66 Thayer Expedition to Brazil, Paulino’s gesture aimed to restore the woman’s humanity and history from a set of photographs made to substantiate claims of racial degeneration supposedly caused by racial mixing.

At a 2018 retrospective at the Pinacoteca de São Paulo, Paulino debuted a series of drawings from the early 2000s that anticipate the psychological exploration seen later in the goddesses of Senhora das Plantas .” Marked by restless lines, these works depict a woman tentatively emerging from a cocoon in a ritual of transformation and emancipation. “Drawing is a central foundation of Rosana’s practice; it sheds light on her imagination. Forms and ideas that she develops through drawing later acquire spatiality,” Valéria Piccoli, the exhibition’s cocurator, told ARTnews . “It was important to emphasize that she was the first voice in the 1990s to speak about the issue of Black women, but also to highlight that this was part of a much broader context of her interests and desires.”

Less than a year later, she would show the earliest iteration of her botanical goddesses. A different sensibility had emerged: The figures, drawn in earth tones, were nude, but the hypersexualization of the Black female body was nowhere to be found. Instead, the works suggested a new way of conceiving wisdom and communion with nature. The series has its roots in the plants Paulino keeps in her studio. Before she named them goddesses, she initially called the plants in the series’ early works “folhas” (leaves).

“I gradually realized that it couldn’t be that simple: plants have a history, so I began to approach them more specifically,” Paulino explained in a recent interview in her studio, noting that she began the series because she could find no Black goddesses in books devoted to the sacred feminine.

She started first with snake plants ( Espada de Iansã in Portuguese). “Then I turned my attention to the jatobá tree,” she added. Works from the series soon appeared in the world’s two oldest recurring exhibitions: the 2022 and 2026 Venice Biennales and the 2023 Bienal de São Paulo. For São Paulo, Paulino moved from watercolor on paper to painting on canvas, scaling her drawings up to nearly 9 feet by 20 feet. Next, she introduced the mangrove. The goddesses in these paintings have a serene air, with roots firmly anchored in the earth, but also a crown of leaves that sway with the wind.

This year, her investigation into Comigo Ninguém Pode (scientifically known as Dieffenbachia ), a toxic plant also associated with spiritual protection, lend the Brazilian Pavilion its title. The pavilion’s curator Diane Lima first saw the works at Mendes Wood DM’s New York space, which had “the day and night series, in which Rosana paints and draws against a black background. I had never seen these works in person before. They convey a sense of mystery and magic; there is a certain aurality to them that truly moves us,” she said of her decision to include work form this series in Venice. “And it had that same impact in Italy. It is the exhibition’s great amulet, and it’s no coincidence that it is positioned right at the entrance.”

Approaching them as if she is still drawing at a table, Paulino lays flat her canvases, which she prepares with gesso mixture to seals the weave so they behave more like paper when she adds watercolor and acrylic on their surfaces. Her decision to work horizontally, however, also reflects a conceptual choice. “I’m not going to reproduce the watercolor brushstrokes on canvas. But at the same time, this idea of vertical painting is very Western. […] My thing is to work on a table,” she said.

Her plant goddesses have recently become more ambiguous as she has become interested in species that thrive in shade or offer it, like Comigo Ninguém Pode. And Paulino’s research into plantas de poder (plants of power), used for spiritual protection in Afro-Brazilian religious traditions, has only deepened, the relationship between her plants and the cycles of day and night becoming more expansive.

In Paris, she will show what she is calling “nocturnal” canvases featuring new goddesses—or new versions of existing ones—associated with angel’s trumpet ( Brugmansia ). A genus known for its exuberant flowers in a range of colors—white, salmon, purple, lilac, pink—they possess a particular luminosity that makes the petals seem, in a sense, translucent. Their alluring quality belies their extreme toxicity; at times used as a hallucinogen, their ingestion can cause severe mental confusion and even death.

Paulino is drawn to this duality: “It’s a plant with a certain weight to it—a size, a scent. But it’s one of the most dangerous plants there is. Many people have lost their lives after ingesting teas containing it.” In Angel’s trumpet (2026), a figure sits on the ground, roots dangling from her knees. Branches emerge from her eyes, bearing the plant’s trumpet-shaped flowers. In her seduction, this goddess exudes strength. An untitled 2026 work, featuring a bromeliad goddess, inhabits a different atmosphere. The seated figure twists her torso in a yoga-like pose, while leaves emerge from her mouth as if she had been chattering animatedly. Her expression is gentle, and her hair cropped short, with a texture resembling tightly coiled hair. Paulino achieved this effect using a tool she made herself: a branch with a sponge attached to its tip.

“You don’t need long, flowing hair to be a goddess,” she said. “My series ‘Senhoras das Plantas’ exists because woman is an archetype that the West cannot fully comprehend,” the artist concludes.

article_text:
Born in 1951 in Lexington, Virginia, where she still lives and works, Sally Mann has made the American South, with its landscapes, its ghosts and its history of violence, the subject of a body of work spanning more than four decades. She first drew wide attention with At Twelve (1988), portraits of adolescent girls, then with Immediate Family (1992), intimate and sometimes unsettling images of her three children growing up on the family farm, which brought her both fame and fierce controversy. Working with an 8×10 view camera, she later turned to the 19th-century wet-plate collodion process, whose flaws, streaks and accidents became part of her vocabulary in series such as “Deep South” and “What Remains,” a meditation on death and decay. In 2015, she published Hold Still , a memoir that was a finalist for the National Book Award. Her retrospective “A Thousand Crossings” opened at the National Gallery of Art in Washington in 2018 before traveling to the Jeu de Paume in Paris in 2019.

This segment comes from “Place,” an episode of the first season of Art21’s documentary series “Art in the Twenty-First Century,” which premiered on PBS in September 2001. Filmed both in her studio and outdoors, it follows Mann at work on the farm where she lives, which serves as both the backdrop and the subject of her photographs.

15 minutes, in English.

article_text:
Johnny Depp reunited with the cast of Ebenezer for the London premiere of the comedy-thriller at the Odeon Luxe Leicester Square.

Joining Depp at the global premiere were Rupert Grint, Tramell Tillman, Sam Claflin, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Robert Strange and Freddie Lee-Grey.

Also on the red carpet were director Ti West, producer Emma Watts and writer Nathaniel Halpern.

RELATED: Soul Train Awards 2026 Red Carpet Photos: Chaka Khan, Common, LisaRaye McCoy & More

Other recognizable stars at the premiere included Minnie Driver, Big Brother UK’s Jedward and Love Island’s Ekin-Su Cülcüloğlu.

Depp stars as the unpleasant Ebenezer Scrooge in a reimagining of Charles Dickens’ A Christmas Carol . On one unforgettable Christmas Eve, Ebenezer collides with his past, present, and future on a supernatural journey that will decide his ultimate fate. If you think you know his story, think again.

Directed by Ti West and written by Nathaniel Halpern, Ebenezer stars Rupert Grint, Andrea Riseborough, Sam Claflin, Daisy Ridley, Arthur Conti, Ellie Bamber, Henry Lloyd-Hughes, Charlie Murphy, Tramell Tillman, and Ian McKellen.

RELATED: Daytime Emmy Awards 2026 Photos: Best Of The Red Carpet

Ebenezer is executive produced by Ti West, Adam Bohling, David Reid, Stephen Deuters, Jason Forman, Pete Chiappetta, Anthony Tittanegro, Andrew Lary, Molly Smith, Thad Luckinbill, Trent Luckinbill. The film is produced by Emma Watts.

The film, which opens in theaters on November 13, is rated PG-13 for frightening material.

RELATED: ‘The Gilded Age’ Season 4 Red Carpet Photos: Carrie Coon, Morgan Spector, Denée Benton, Cynthia Nixon & More

article_text:
Série tem estreia prevista para 13 de outubro pelo streaming Disney+.

Durante seu painel na conferência D23, a Marvel divulgou o primeiro trailer de “ VisionQuest “, série que conclui a trilogia iniciada em “WandaVision” em 2019. Assista acima (legendado).

Assista abaixo à versão dublada.

Foi divulgado também o primeiro cartaz internacional da série, abaixo.

“VisionQuest” chega quase dois anos após “Agatha Desde Sempre” e cinco anos e meio após o fim de “WandaVision”, enfim completando a jornada do casal Wanda Maximoff/Feiticeira Escarlate e o Visão após os eventos de “Vingadores: Ultimato”. Ao longo da trilogia, novos personagens são apresentados, como os filhos gêmeos da dupla, Billy e Tommy Maximoff, e a bruxa Agatha Harkness.

Em “VisionQuest”, o Visão tem vivido escondido após ser reinicializado em “WandaVision” e escapar da agência S.W.O.R.D., que pretendia transformá-lo em uma arma. Em busca de um novo propósito, ele consulta as personalidades de IA incorporadas à sua programação, incluindo F.R.I.D.A.Y., E.D.I.T.H., J.A.R.V.I.S. e o infame Ultron. Sua existência discreta chega ao fim quando uma recompensa por sua cabeça o força a fugir na companhia de Thomas Shepard, um garoto misterioso que pode ser a reencarnação de Tommy Maximoff, um dos filhos do Visão. Enquanto tenta escapar da captura, o Visão precisa confrontar sua própria natureza, resistir à influência de Ultron e desvendar o enigma que é seu jovem companheiro para conseguir sobreviver.

O elenco é liderado por Paul Bettany no papel do Visão, com James Spader retomando o papel de Ultron. Demais nomes incluem Todd Stashwick, Faran Tahir, Lauren Morais, Diane Morgan, Orla Brady, Polly Frame, Henry Lewis, Jonathan Sayer, Emily Hampshire e James D’Arcy.

“VisionQuest” tem estreia prevista para 13 de outubro pelo streaming Disney+.

article_text:
Films and events

First Feature Competition

Ben’Imana

This Cannes Camera d’Or winner unfolds in the shadow of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, exploring its legacy and the possibility of forgiveness.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo

Screenwriters Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo, Delphine Agut

With Clémentine U. Nyirinkindi, Isabelle Kabano, Kesia Kelly Nishimwe

Rwanda-France-Gabon-Norway 2026. 101min

Courtesy of Alexander

Language Kinyarwanda With English subtitles

Introduction

A survivor of the Rwandan genocide tries to lead her community toward reconciliation and to foster dialogue between victims and the families of perpetrators. Generations of women share different perspectives as they confront their trauma together, in an intimate and thoughtful film about resilience, sisterhood and communal healing.

Isabel Moir

Content advice

Contains scenes of sexual violence.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

Lady

In a bustling Lagos, a solitary female taxi driver finds community among a group of sex workers as she transports them around the city.

Variations on a Theme

The Tiger Award winner at this year’s Rotterdam Film Festival is a gentle and enchanting portrait of an octogenarian goat herder in South Africa’s Kamiesberge.

House of the Wind

Cameroonian director Bernard Auguste Kouemo Yanghu’s outstanding feature debut is a poignant tale of an ageing parent who has been left behind.

article_text:
In Memoriam

Artist and Gallerist Peter Nagy, Who Shaped Two Art Scenes, Dies at 66

We honor a fixture of New York and New Delhi art, a painter who folded the world into abstraction, and a champion of Denver’s scene in this week's column memorializing those we recently lost in the art world.

In Memoriam honors those we recently lost in the art world.

Peter Nagy (1959–2026) Artist and gallerist who shaped art scenes in New York and New Delhi

He co-founded the East Village gallery Nature Morte in 1982, one of the earliest artist-run galleries in the neighborhood, which showed artists such as Louise Lawler, Gretchen Bender, and Keith Sonnier during its six-year run. He fell in love with India and its art in 1992, reopening Nature Morte in New Delhi five years later, helping to build the city's gallery system.

An accomplished artist in his own right, his post-conceptualist work merged painting with photocopy technology. International Survey Condominiums (1985), for instance, wove art-historical timelines with museum floorplans. His work is held in the collections of the Whitney Museum, the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Los Angeles Museum of Contemporary Art, and more.

"Art may always be about art," Nagy wrote in a catalog essay, "but the best is also about life and life seems to be about themes which take us in and out of ourselves, on travels far away and ultimately back home again."

editorial_title_zh: 新篇章：蔡茨当代艺术博物馆宣布埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞担任艺术总监
editorial_excerpt_zh: 8月12日星期三，蔡茨当代艺术博物馆宣布西班牙策展人埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞（Elvira Dyangani Ose）为艺术总监。埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞曾任巴塞罗那当代艺术博物馆（MACBA）馆长。[...]
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Artthrob于2026年8月12日发布的新闻。阅读本文大约需要2分钟。", "links": [{"text": "news item", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/category/primary/news/"}, {"text": "Artthrob", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/article-author/artthrob/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "蔡茨当代艺术博物馆", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "8月12日星期三，蔡茨当代艺术博物馆宣布西班牙策展人埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞担任艺术总监。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞曾任巴塞罗那当代艺术博物馆（MACBA）馆长。她曾担任伦敦The Showroom总监兼首席策展人、伦敦大学金史密斯学院视觉文化讲师以及普拉达基金会思想委员会成员。她此前还曾担任哥德堡国际当代艺术双年展策展人；伦敦泰特现代美术馆国际艺术策展人；刚果民主共和国卢本巴希双年展（Rencontres Picha）艺术总监；塞维利亚安达卢西亚当代艺术中心（CAAC）当代艺术策展人；纽约Creative Time高级策展人；以及大加那利岛拉斯帕尔马斯大西洋现代艺术中心（CAAM）当代艺术策展人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "蔡茨当代艺术博物馆联合创始人兼联席主席大卫·格林（David Green OBE）评论道：“经过广泛的本地和国际搜寻，董事会非常高兴地欢迎埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞加入蔡茨当代艺术博物馆。迪扬加尼·奥塞的任命体现了我们作为一家机构的定位——立足非洲，连结世界。她将监督博物馆的策展愿景与方向，引领该机构迈向即将迎来第二个十年的新篇章——延续已故的科约·库奥（Koyo Kouoh）的遗志，致敬她非凡的艺术愿景以及她所奠定的机构基础。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "蔡茨当代艺术博物馆联合创始人兼联席主席约根·蔡茨（Jochen Zeitz）补充道：“迪扬加尼·奥塞在我们的发展历程中的关键时刻加入蔡茨当代艺术博物馆。在我们即将迎来10周年之际，她的任命建立在我们第一个十年所奠定的基础之上。她带来了深厚的机构领导经验，并将拓展博物馆在展览、研究、收藏、公众参与以及我们与艺术家和观众合作方式等方面的艺术雄心。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在谈到自己的任命时，埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞表示：“加入蔡茨当代艺术博物馆是一种荣幸。我很激动能在此时加入，继续其作为具有全球影响力的非洲领先机构的征程。我期待与博物馆杰出的团队、艺术家、支持者以及本地和全球社区并肩作战，通过在不同文化和地域之间促进有意义的合作与艺术交流，在其非凡的基石上继续前行。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "埃尔维拉·迪扬加尼·奥塞将于2026年10月1日正式履新。", "translated": true}]

This should take you 2 minutes to read.", "links": [{"text": "news item", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/category/primary/news/"}, {"text": "Artthrob", "url": "https://artthrob.co.za/article-author/artthrob/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Zeitz MOCAA"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "On Wednesday, 12 August, Zeitz MOCAA announced Spanish curator Elvira Dyangani Ose as artistic director."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Elvira Dyangani Ose served as the director of the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona (MACBA). She was the director and chief curator of The Showroom in London, as well as a lecturer in Visual Cultures at Goldsmiths, University of London, and a member of the Thought Council, Fondazione Prada. She has previously been curator of the Göteborg International Biennial of Contemporary Art; curator of international art at Tate Modern, London; artistic director of Rencontres Picha – Lubumbashi Biennial, Democratic Republic of the Congo; curator of contemporary art at the Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo (CAAC), Seville; senior curator at Creative Time in New York; and curator of contemporary art at the Centro Atlántico de Arte Moderno (CAAM) in Las Palmas, Gran Canaria."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Zeitz MOCAA Co-founder and Co-chair, David Green OBE, commented: ‘Following an extensive local and international search, the Board is delighted to welcome Elvira Dyangani Ose to Zeitz MOCAA. Dyangani Ose’s appointment reflects who we are as an institution—one rooted in Africa, while connected to the world . She will oversee the Museum’s curatorial vision and direction, leading the institution through its next chapter as it approaches its second decade—building on the late Koyo Kouoh’s legacy , and honouring her extraordinary artistic vision and the institutional foundations she built.’"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Adding to this, Jochen Zeitz , Zeitz MOCAA Co-founder and Co-chair said: ‘Dyangani Ose joins Zeitz MOCAA at a defining moment in our journey. As we approach our 10th anniversary, her appointment builds on the foundations laid in our first decade. article_text:
A news item by Artthrob on the 12th of August 2026. This should take you 2 minutes to read.

Zeitz MOCAA

On Wednesday, 12 August, Zeitz MOCAA announced Spanish curator Elvira Dyangani Ose as artistic director.

Elvira Dyangani Ose served as the director of the Museu d’Art Contemporani de Barcelona (MACBA). She was the director and chief curator of The Showroom in London, as well as a lecturer in Visual Cultures at Goldsmiths, University of London, and a member of the Thought Council, Fondazione Prada. She has previously been curator of the Göteborg International Biennial of Contemporary Art; curator of international art at Tate Modern, London; artistic director of Rencontres Picha – Lubumbashi Biennial, Democratic Republic of the Congo; curator of contemporary art at the Centro Andaluz de Arte Contemporáneo (CAAC), Seville; senior curator at Creative Time in New York; and curator of contemporary art at the Centro Atlántico de Arte Moderno (CAAM) in Las Palmas, Gran Canaria.

Zeitz MOCAA Co-founder and Co-chair, David Green OBE, commented: ‘Following an extensive local and international search, the Board is delighted to welcome Elvira Dyangani Ose to Zeitz MOCAA. Dyangani Ose’s appointment reflects who we are as an institution—one rooted in Africa, while connected to the world . She will oversee the Museum’s curatorial vision and direction, leading the institution through its next chapter as it approaches its second decade—building on the late Koyo Kouoh’s legacy , and honouring her extraordinary artistic vision and the institutional foundations she built.’

Adding to this, Jochen Zeitz , Zeitz MOCAA Co-founder and Co-chair said: ‘Dyangani Ose joins Zeitz MOCAA at a defining moment in our journey. As we approach our 10th anniversary, her appointment builds on the foundations laid in our first decade. She brings deep experience in institutional leadership and will expand the museum’s artistic ambition—across exhibitions, research, collections, public engagement, and the way we work with artists and audiences.’

Commenting on her appointment, Elvira Dyangani Ose said: ‘It is a privilege to join Zeitz MOCAA. I am thrilled to come on board at this moment to continue its journey as a leading African institution with global reach. I look forward to working alongside the museum’s remarkable team, artists, supporters, and the local and global communities, building upon its extraordinary foundation by fostering meaningful collaborations and artistic exchanges across cultures and geographies.’

Elvira Dyangani Ose will begin her term on 1 October 2026.

article_text:
France’s Luxbox and Spain’s Amore Cine have boarded the Peruvian drama “Portrait Huaco” (“Huaco retrato”) by Melina León, best known for her debut feature “Song Without a Name” (“Canción sin nombre”), which world premiered at the 2019 Cannes Directors’ Fortnight.

“ After the incredible journey we shared with ‘Song Without a Name,’ I’m thrilled to continue collaborating with Melina, now as both international sales agent and co-producer,” said Luxbox’s Fiorella Moretti.

She added: “As a Peruvian, it is especially meaningful to help bring Gabriela Wiener’s bold and contemporary work to the screen through Melina’s singular vision. ‘Portrait Huaco’ explores questions at the heart of today’s conversations in a truly original way, and I have no doubt it will resonate with audiences around the world.”

For Paz Lázaro, who co-founded Amore Cine alongside Edson Sidonie (“Karnawal”) and Juan Pablo Felix (“Mil pedazos”), “Adapting Gabriela Wiener’s ‘Portrait Huaco’ means bringing to the screen a work that bridges Latin America and Spain, weaving colonialism, racism, identity and desire with a voice both ancient and radically contemporary.”

“For Amore Cine, alongside our fellow producing partners, this is an opportunity to champion a film with international reach that challenges perspectives and reexamines our shared history.”

Based on the autobiographical novel of the Peruvian author, the project participates in the 8th Proyecta Co-Production Forum at Ventana Sur , which takes place in Montevideo, Uruguay this year from Nov. 30 – Dec. 4.

Amore Cine and Luxbox join Peru’s Mano de Obra Cine, led by Melissa Cordero, and La Vida Misma Films, which produced “Song Without a Name.”

The story follows Gabriela who returns to Lima after her father dies. Back home, she discovers a book by her great-great-grandfather, Austrian explorer Charles Wiener. Her search into the family past becomes a reckoning with the lingering legacies of colonialism, internalized racism and abandonment.

“’Portrait Huaco’ combines a distinctly Peruvian perspective with universal themes of identity, memory and colonial heritage. Under the direction of Melina León, the film seeks to preserve its cultural roots and Peruvian creative leadership while embracing an international scope through strategic co-production partnerships,” said Cordero.

This is the second time for Mano de Obra to co-produce with Amore Cine. Late coming-of-age drama, “Ofelia,” currently in post,’ is a European-Latin American co-production that includes Amore, Argentina’s Bikini Films, Quijote Films of Chile, Brazil’s África Filmes and CUP Filmes, Spain’s Potenza Producciones and France’s Reality Films.

Said Cordero: “I’m interested in producing auteur-driven films with a distinctive cinematic voice and strong cultural identity, as well as genre films that can connect with wider audiences. I’m particularly drawn to stories rooted in Peru and Latin America that explore universal themes, bringing local perspectives to an international audience.”

“My near-term strategy is to strengthen Mano de Obra Cine’s position as a production company focused on feature films, building strategic co-production partnerships across Latin America and Europe. I aim to combine public and private financing with international partnerships and distribution opportunities to develop a sustainable slate of films with strong creative identities and international reach.”

Jack Begert ’s directorial debut JUNK , starring David Schwimmer , Dominic Fike , Talia Ryder , Jena Malone and Gaby Hoffman is now streaming on Mubi.

Begert, known for directing many a music video for the likes of Olivia Rodrigo, Kendrick Lamar, Jack Harlow, Doja Cat, Dominic Fike and more, describes the film as “a portrait of people caught up in escapism, addiction, and a crisis of meaning.”

article_text:
“The Batman” star Robert Pattinson has offered his first comments after the highly anticipated DC superhero sequel had to pause production last week . Matt Reeves , who is returning to direct the follow-up, had to step away from production due to a “family matter.”

“We’re pausing for a little bit and then we’re going to figure it all out,” Pattinson told the Official Pop Drop at the London Film Festival’s U.K. premiere of his new film “Primetime.”

Related Stories

Kevin Delaney Takes Role as NBC News' Head of Digital Content and Subscription

On Oct. 5, news broke that Reeves needed to take a step back from filming; no reason has been given for his leave nor has there been any update on if “The Batman Part II” will need to shift its release date from Feb. 18, 2028.

“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement last Monday. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”

Along with Pattinson, other cast members for “The Batman Part II” include Scarlett Johansson, Sebastian Stan, Charles Dance, Brian Tyree Henry, Colin Farrell as the Penguin, Andy Serkis as Alfred Pennyworth and Jeffrey Wright as Commissioner Gordon.

It’s been a long journey for “The Batman” sequel, with several delays along the way. The movie was first slated to release on Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it a year to Oct. 1, 2027. Then, the studio pushed the film to February 2028. Reeves and Pattinson’s first “Batman” was released on March 4, 2022, meaning the sequel will land six years after the original.
